title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Zone I Flexor Digitorum Profundus Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Last 25 Years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Zone I flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon injuries, at the distal phalanx insertion, generally require surgery. However, outcomes may vary, and multiple surgical techniques have been described. This review sought to evaluate management, rehabilitation, and outcomes following zone I FDP injuries.
METHODS: Using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, a systematic review and meta-analysis was performed. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane were queried for articles concerning zone I FDP injuries since 2000. Patients younger than 18 years of age and revision surgery were excluded. Demographics, strength, range of motion, outcome scores, therapy protocols, and complications were evaluated.
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria and were stratified by treatment strategy into 31 cohorts comprising 669 fingers. The mean age was 36 years and 25% were women. Injury mechanisms included 348 lacerations (52%) and 234 avulsions (35%); 88 injuries (13%) were unspecified. Primary tenorrhaphy was the most frequently reported treatment (39%), followed by tenorrhaphy with a tie-over button (10%) and bone anchor fixation (10%). The mean time to surgery was 4 days. Range of motion or outcome measures were documented in 12 cohorts (39%) and strength in 10 cohorts (32%). Meta-analysis demonstrated postoperative FDP rupture, revision surgery, and tenolysis rates of 2.0%, 1.0%, and 1.6%, respectively. Lacerations were treated with primary tenorrhaphy more commonly compared with avulsions (59% vs 22%) and had higher revision rates (7.6% vs 1.4%).
CONCLUSIONS: Surgical repair of zone I FDP injuries demonstrates low complication rates and generally favorable outcomes; however, inconsistent reporting of functional outcomes limits meaningful comparison between surgical techniques.

title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing.
STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5.
RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes.
METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements.
CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach.
STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey.
METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing.
RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria.
DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions.
CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort.
METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score).
RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed.
DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

title: Associations between mental health conditions and outcomes of pain and function following upper extremity fragility fractures: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Upper extremity fragility fractures (UEFF) are increasingly prevalent among older adults and are associated with functional decline, recurrent fracture risk, and increased mortality. While physical comorbidities influence recovery, the impact of pre-existing mental health conditions on pain and function following UEFF is less clear.
PURPOSE: To synthesize evidence examining associations between pre-existing mental health conditions and pain and functional outcomes following UEFF.
STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, PEDro, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies included adults with UEFF that assessed mental health conditions (eg, depression, anxiety, and pain catastrophizing) identified prior to or within 2 weeks of fracture and reported pain or functional outcomes using validated measures. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. Due to substantial heterogeneity in psychological constructs, outcome measures, and follow-up intervals, findings were synthesized narratively by short- (≤3 months), mid- (6-9 months), and long-term (≥12 months) follow-up.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included [10 distal radius fractures (DRF), three proximal humerus fractures (PHF)]. In DRF, short‑term outcomes were primarily associated with anxiety and pain catastrophizing, which predicted poorer grip strength, range of motion, and upper‑extremity functional performance. Mid‑term outcomes were influenced by psychological distress, pain interference, fear of movement, and self‑efficacy. At long‑term follow‑up, depression was the most consistent predictor of persistent disability, with affected individuals demonstrating worse functional scores and slower recovery trajectories. Antidepressant use and registry‑defined common mental disorders present before fracture were associated with poorer long‑term outcomes. In PHF, pre‑existing mental health diagnoses and kinesiophobia were associated with worse mid‑ to long‑term disability and quality‑of‑life outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Pre-existing mental health conditions are important prognostic factors for pain and functional recovery following UEFF. Incorporating early psychosocial screening and psychologically informed rehabilitation may improve outcomes.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement in American football athletes: examining factors associated with outcomes at a mean follow-up time of 6.3 years.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAIS) is a common cause of hip pain and performance limitation in athletes. Hip arthroscopy is the gold standard of treatment in professional American football athletes, with numerous studies demonstrating favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport (RTS) rates. However, limited outcomes data exists in collegiate athletes and fewer still in high school athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term patient-reported outcomes (PROs), RTS rates, and predictors of outcomes following hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS in high school and collegiate football athletes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed which included high-school and collegiate football athletes who underwent hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS. Outcomes were assessed using the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), International Hip Outcome Tool-12 (IHOT-12), and Hip Outcomes Score-Sport Specific Subscale (HOS-Sport). Data regarding return to preinjury sport were also collected. Pre-operative radiographic data, including alpha angle, lateral center edge angle, and Tönnis grade, were collected.
RESULTS: This cohort had a mean post-operative follow up of 6.3 years, with mean PRO scores of 82.2 on the mHHS, 84.6 on the iHOT-12, and 88.3 on the HOS-Sport. PASS thresholds were achieved by 69%, 77% and 80% of athletes for the same outcomes, respectively. 60% of the cohort attempted to return to sport, and 91% of the athletes who attempted to return to preinjury level of sport were successful. Increased age at time of surgery and larger pre-operative alpha angles were associated with worse PRO scores at follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Hip arthroscopy for FAIS in high school and collegiate football players yielded favorable long-term outcomes and RTS rates. This is similar to current outcomes data in professional athletes. Increased alpha angle and age at surgery were associated with worse outcomes, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and appropriate surgical treatment. Comparisons of outcomes between blocking and nonblocking positions may warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

title: Rehabilitation strategies for carpal instability: A scoping review of conservative and postsurgical interventions.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Carpal instability can cause pain, weakness, mechanical symptoms, and long-term disability. Rehabilitation is central to both conservative care and post-surgical recovery, yet clinicians face fragmented evidence.
PURPOSE: To map and synthesize rehabilitation strategies for carpal instability across conservative and postsurgical pathways, and to identify gaps that limit evidence-informed practice.
STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review.
METHODS: JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines were followed. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, with no date restrictions, up to March 16, 2026. Findings were summarized numerically and thematically and interpreted using an ICF-oriented taxonomy.
RESULTS: Fifty-nine reports published between 1990 and 2025 were included. The literature was methodologically heterogeneous, largely composed of descriptive or secondary designs. Reports addressed conservative rehabilitation, post-surgical rehabilitation, or both, with dissociative (CID) and non-dissociative (CIND) carpal instability being the most frequently addressed patterns. Rehabilitation strategies identified across the included literature were categorized into six categories: immobilization; pain/edema/scar, and education-related management; mobilization; therapeutic exercise; proprioceptive training; and instrumental/physical modalities. Immobilization and therapeutic exercise were the most frequently described components. Rehabilitation strategies varied by instability type, particularly in orthotic selection and muscle recruitment. Pain, function, strength, and range of motion were the most frequently reported outcomes, while participation-level outcomes such as return to work or sport were inconsistently addressed. Dosage, treatment progression criteria, and follow-up were variably reported across studies.
CONCLUSIONS: This review provides a practical synthesis of recurring rehabilitation components across conservative and post-surgical care that may support rehabilitation planning. It also identifies key reporting gaps in intervention content, dosage, progression criteria, outcomes, and follow-up. The findings encourage a broader interpretation of carpal instability as a condition shaped not only by structural injury, but also by the interaction between passive stabilizing structures, active muscular support, motor control, and the capacity to sustain function under load and during activity.

title: Effects of repeated isometric exercise on pain-related and physical recovery outcomes following exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate repeated quadriceps isometric exercise for recovery following experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes.
DESIGN: Parallel-group, randomized sham-controlled trial.
METHODS: Forty university athletes were randomized to isometric exercise (n = 20) or sham exercise (n = 20). Co-primary outcomes were pressure pain threshold and soreness intensity; secondary outcomes were knee flexion range of motion, quadriceps isometric strength, and thigh circumference. Assessments occurred before and immediately after soreness induction and on Days 1, 3, and 5. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for soreness (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.898), pressure pain threshold (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.745), and knee flexion range of motion (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.378). Soreness was lower in the isometric group on Day 1 (mean difference, -2.55 points; 95% confidence interval -3.00 to -2.10; Hedges' g = -3.19) and Day 3 (-1.90 points; 95% confidence interval -2.35 to -1.45; Hedges' g = -2.74). Pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed no significant between-group differences at individual time points. Group × Time interactions were not significant for quadriceps strength or thigh circumference.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated submaximal isometric exercise was associated with lower perceived soreness during peak symptoms. Although pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed different temporal patterns, neither differed significantly between groups at individual time points. Benefits for physical recovery outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class.
RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

title: Autologous Osteochondral Transplantation Remains a Reliable Option for Talar Osteochondral Lesions, With Low Knee Donor-Site Morbidity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral transplantation (AOT) is a surgical option for talar osteochondral lesions (OCL), with favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport rates; however, knee donor-site morbidity remains a concern.
PURPOSE: To evaluate clinical and functional outcomes, complications, return to work and sport, and satisfaction after AOT for talar OCL.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective case series.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients ≥18 years with talar OCL treated with AOT (2011-2022; minimum 2-year follow-up); patients with prior knee pain or surgery, infection, advanced osteoarthritis, or rheumatologic disease were excluded. Outcomes included the AOFAS hindfoot, Lysholm, and Tegner scores, ankle and knee visual analog scale (VAS) pain, satisfaction, return to work and sport, and complications.
RESULTS: Thirty-seven patients (78% male; median age, 36 years; median follow-up, 24 months) were included. Median lesion size was 150 mm², all medial; 14 (38%) had concomitant procedures. The AOFAS score improved from 54.5 to 95.8 (mean difference, 41.3; 95% CI, 38.4-44.3) and ankle VAS from 7.0 to 1.6 (-5.4; 95% CI, -5.9 to -4.9) (both p < 0.001). Postoperative Lysholm score was 98.8 ± 4.0 and knee VAS 1.2 ± 0.8 (no preoperative knee scores). Return to work took 2.3 ± 1.2 months; all 32 athletes resumed sport at 6.5 ± 2.1 months, 20 (63%) in their pre-injury sport. Tegner scores were unchanged (5.4 vs 5.5; p = 0.624). One knee hemarthrosis and one repeat ankle arthroscopy occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: AOT for talar OCL yielded favorable short-term outcomes, high return-to-work and return-to-sport rates, and low reported knee donor-site morbidity; baseline knee scores were unavailable.
LEVEL OF CLINICAL EVIDENCE: 4.

title: The Impact of Tourniquet Duration on Postoperative Opioid Use and Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tourniquet use during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains common, but its effects on postoperative pain, opioid use, and stiffness are unclear. We evaluated whether tourniquet duration was associated with pain- and stiffness-related outcomes after primary TKA.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective study of 17,850 adults undergoing primary unilateral TKA at a single center from March 2016 to June 2023. Tourniquet use was categorized by inflation time relative to operative time as no tourniquet (n = 1,243), partial tourniquet (less than 0.6; n = 2,914), tourniquet-until-arthrotomy-closure (≥ 0.6 to less than 1; n = 10,003), or full-duration tourniquet (≥ 1; n = 3,690). The primary outcome was postoperative pain assessed by postoperative inpatient and cumulative 90-day morphine milligram equivalents (MME). The secondary outcomes were hours to clear physical therapy (PT), manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) within 120 days, and patient-reported Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) at six weeks. Multivariable regressions adjusted for covariates. The no-tourniquet group served as the reference.
RESULTS: Partial-tourniquet use was associated with lower 90-day opioid consumption (-90 MME; 95% confidence interval (CI) -150 to -30; P = 0.003). Tourniquet-until-closure and full-duration tourniquet were associated with higher inpatient opioid consumption (+10 MMEs; 95% CI, 2 to 17; P = 0.015; and +14 MMEs; 95% CI, 6 to 22; P = 0.001), longer time to PT clearance (+2.7 hours, 95% CI, 1.0 to 4.5; P = 0.002; and +4.1 hours, 95% CI, 2.2 to 5.9; P < 0.001), and higher adjusted odds (OR) of MUA (OR 1.78, 95% CI, 1.14 to 2.79; P = 0.012; and OR 1.64, 95% CI, 1.02 to 2.64; P = 0.040). Partial-tourniquet use was not associated with increased time to clear PT or increased odds of MUA. The KOOS JR scores did not differ significantly across strategies.
CONCLUSIONS: Tourniquet use during TKA showed duration-dependent associations with postoperative outcomes. Partial-tourniquet use may represent a balanced strategy, associated with lower cumulative 90-day opioid consumption without the delayed PT clearance or increased MUA risk observed with longer-duration tourniquet strategies.

title: Beyond Morphology: Quantitative Bilateral Self-Referenced Frequency-Domain Diffuse Optical Spectroscopy Reveals Functional Abnormalities in Patellar Tendinopathy.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Patellar tendinopathy (PT) involves functional and metabolic abnormalities that may precede structural degeneration, whereas MRI and ultrasonography primarily depict morphology. To bridge this gap, we aim to develop a quantitative optical method for detecting PT-related functional and hemodynamic abnormalities.
METHODS: We developed an embedded multi-wavelength frequency-domain diffuse optical spectroscopy system integrating sinusoidal modulation, synchronized acquisition, real-time Goertzel demodulation, optical-property inversion, chromophore fitting, and standardized grid scanning over the patellar tendon region. To reduce inter-subject variability, a bilateral self-referenced strategy used the contralateral tendon as an endogenous reference. A composite optical biomarker, Tendon Hemodynamic Index (THI), was defined by integrating differential tissue oxygenation and blood-volume-related information.
RESULTS: Phantom and in vivo measurements demonstrated robust quantitative performance. In a clinical cohort, THI was significantly elevated in PT patients and correlated with symptom severity and functional impairment across the full cohort, with Spearman correlations of 0.69 with the Numeric Rating Scale and -0.74 with the Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment-Patella score. In this exploratory cohort, THI distinguished PT from healthy controls with 91.8% accuracy, 95.8% sensitivity, 88.0% specificity, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.928. In imaging negative but symptom-positive cases, THI achieved 88.2% classification accuracy. In three exploratory follow-up cases, THI decreased toward the bilateral baseline as symptoms improved over 8 weeks.
CONCLUSION: The proposed method enables self-referenced quantification of PT-related functional abnormalities.
SIGNIFICANCE: By revealing tendon hemodynamic abnormalities beyond structural imaging, this work supports early PT detection, objective severity assessment, and quantitative monitoring of disease recovery.

title: Breast Injuries in Women's Rugby Union: A Comparison of Prospective and Retrospective Surveillance.
abstract: Retrospective research has reported a high prevalence of breast injuries in women's rugby union (RU); however, most injuries are not reported to medical staff. This study compared the incidence and severity of breast injuries collected both prospectively and retrospectively over a comparable match exposure period. Prospective surveillance was conducted by clinicians (n = 14) using an online injury surveillance system across 140 RU players. Retrospective surveillance was conducted using an anonymous online survey completed by 370 RU players. Injury incidence was calculated per 1000 hours of match exposure. Severity was assessed using breast pain, bruising and swelling, ability to continue play, perceived effect on performance, and long-term breast changes. Three breast injuries were prospectively recorded over 1204 hours of competition (2.5 injuries/1000 hours). In contrast, 144 breast injuries were reported retrospectively over 5055 hours of competition (28.5 injuries/1000 hours). The retrospective injury rate was significantly higher than the prospective rate (IRR = 11.4, 95% CI: 3.15-41.73; p < 0.002). Ninety-six percent (n = 139) of retrospectively reported injuries had not been disclosed to medical staff. Injury severity was similar between surveillance methods, with bruising commonly reported, all players continuing to participate despite injury, and over half perceiving a negative effect on performance. Long-term breast changes were reported by 6% (n = 8) of players. The substantially lower incidence recorded prospectively suggests that breast injuries are underreported in women's RU. Improved reporting and surveillance strategies are required to better capture breast injuries and support female athlete health and performance.

title: Investigation of reaction time in children with brachial plexus birth injuries: A controlled study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Brachial plexus birth injury (BPBI) results in musculoskeletal impairments, sensory deficits, and central nervous system alterations that may negatively affect upper extremity function; however, reaction time (RT), which reflects sensorimotor integration, central information processing, and motor response generation, has not been comprehensively investigated in children with BPBI.
PURPOSE: The aim was to compare upper extremity reaction time between the affected and unaffected sides in children with BPBI and healthy controls while examining its relationships with upper extremity performance, sensation, bilateral coordination, balance, activity, participation, and fall frequency.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional case-control study.
METHODS: Seventy-six children with upper trunk BPBI and 72 healthy controls were included. Reaction time was assessed using BlazePod. Active movements were evaluated using the Active Movement Scale (AMS), upper extremity performance with the Box and Block Test (BBT), sensation with the Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Test, bilateral coordination and balance with the Bruininks Oseretsky Motor Proficiency Test, activity and participation with the Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument.
RESULTS: Reaction time was longer on the affected side (555.3±89.5 ms) than the unaffected side (495.9±73.7 ms) and healthy controls (476.2±71.7 ms) (p<0.001). Reaction time showed a strong negative correlation with BBT (r=-0.72, p<0.001), a moderate negative correlation with bilateral coordination (r=-0.51, p<0.001), and a moderate positive correlation with sensation (r=0.42, p<0.001). Weak negative correlations were noted for AMS (r=-0.31, p<0.05) and activity and participation (r=-0.26, p<0.05); however, balance showed no correlation (p=0.12). Children with BPBI had a higher fall frequency than healthy controls (p<0.001), and fall frequency was not associated with reaction time (p>0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: RT is prolonged in the affected extremity in children with BPBI and may negatively affect upper extremity performance and bilateral coordination. Incorporating RT-oriented interventions into rehabilitation may enhance functional and sports performance in children with BPBI.

title: Orthopedic Surgeon and Primary Care Orthopedic Physician Preferences for Sports Participation for Cast-Immobilized Healing Fractures: A Survey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: No published clinical practice guidelines outlining recommended activity restrictions were found for patients with cast-immobilized healing fractures; wide variations in practice exist. This survey aimed to elucidate physician/surgeon preferences for sports participation for patients with short arm cast-immobilized distal radial metaphyseal fractures.
METHODS: Attending orthopedic surgeons, physiatrists, and primary care sports medicine physicians at a single urban tertiary-care orthopedic hospital were invited to complete an anonymous survey with up to 26 questions from 5/2023-7/2023. Descriptive statistics were done. Pearson Chi-Square tests compared pediatric surgeons to all other providers.
RESULTS: One hundred twenty physicians and surgeons were invited to participate. Response rate was 43% (51/120); 59% (30/51) reported treating distal radial fractures with casting and were invited to complete the remaining survey; 70% (21/30) allow return to sports while casted. For respondents permitting sports/activity participation, factors impacting this decision included longer healing time from injury, minimal displacement, greater radiographic healing, and older age at the time of injury. Type of activity, effect on quality of life, level of competition, effect on college/team recruitment, and patient and parental pressure were noted factors impacting activity recommendations. Comparing pediatric orthopedic surgeons with all other providers, there was no notable difference in proportion permitting return to sport/activity in cast (63% vs. 73%, P = 0.67).
CONCLUSION: For cast-immobilized healing fractures of the distal radius, many physicians/surgeons permit sport/activity participation in some capacity, with multiple variables impacting providers preference for activity restrictions. Clinical practice guidelines delineating activity restrictions for cast-immobilized fractures should be developed.

title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection.
PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study.
METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales.
RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.

title: Horizontal and Multidirectional Single-Leg Hop Tests Predict Isokinetic Quadriceps and Hamstring Strengths After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), isokinetic strength and single-leg hop tests (SLHT) are used to assess return to sport readiness. This study examined the relationships and predictive effects of isokinetic knee extension (Ex) and flexion (Flx) strength with 5 SLHTs at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR.
HYPOTHESIS: There would be significant correlation between knee Ex and Flx strengths on the operated side and 5 different SLHTs; SLHTs would significantly predict knee isokinetic Ex and Flx strength.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Fifty-one male participants underwent unilateral ACLR. Lysholm, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), and Tegner scales were assessed preoperatively and 6 to 8 months postoperatively. At the same follow-up, isokinetic strength at 60°/s, 180°/s, and 240°/s and 5 SLHTs were tested on both limbs. Data were analyzed with paired t tests, Pearson correlations, Fisher's exact test, and simple linear regression; limb symmetry index (LSI) cut-off was ≥85%.
RESULTS: Isokinetic strength and single-leg hop (SH), crossover hop, and medial side triple-hop (TH) distances did not differ significantly between limbs (P > 0.05), whereas TH and 90° medial rotation hop distances were significantly shorter on the operated side (P < 0.05). Participants' Lysholm and IKDC scores improved significantly at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR (P < 0.001), but Tegner activity level did not change significantly (P > 0.05). High correlation was found between Ex strength at 60°/s and SH and TH distances on the operated side, and high-moderate correlations were found at 180°/s and 240°/s. Flx strengths showed a similar but slightly lower degree of correlation. Simple linear regression models revealed that especially SH and TH distances significantly predicted both Ex and Flx strengths (adjusted R2 0.26-0.52; P < 0.001). Among the LSI values, only a significant correlation was found between 60°/s Ex and TH LSI ratio (P = 0.01).
CONCLUSION: The findings show that SH and TH tests were highly predictive of isokinetic knee strength after ACLR.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SLHTs after ACLR can be used as a practical and accessible complement to isokinetic measurements.

title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication.
HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff.
STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies.
RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Home-based transcranial direct current stimulation and exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis: A mixed-methods pilot randomised controlled trial.
abstract: This mixed-methods pilot trial evaluated the feasibility and patient perceptions of home-based transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with exercise for pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. Twenty-four participants were allocated to active or sham home-based tDCS plus exercise. Participants completed 10 tDCS sessions over two weeks and an eight-week exercise program, with laboratory assessments at baseline, week four, and week eight. Primary outcomes were recruitment, adherence, adverse events, attrition, and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included local pressure pain thresholds, pain, function, quality of life, and semi-structured interviews exploring intervention facilitators and barriers. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively and qualitative data using inductive thematic analysis. All prespecified feasibility and safety criteria were met. Adherence was high, with 88% of participants (21/24) completing at least 75% of tDCS sessions, and 75% (18/24) completing at least 75% of exercise sessions. No significant adverse events occurred. Mean (SD) pain intensity /100 decreased from 47.3 (25.6) to 28.3 (16.1) in the active group and from 46.4 (17.8) to 33.5 (16.7) in the sham group at week 8. A future trial would require 80 participants. Qualitative themes indicated that evidence of effectiveness was more important to engagement than financial cost, tDCS was viewed as an appealing alternative to pharmacological treatment, and initial device operation was a greater barrier than safety or home use. Home-based tDCS combined with exercise was feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable intervention improves pain and function in people with knee osteoarthritis. PERSPECTIVE: This pilot trial indicates that home-based tDCS combined with exercise is feasible, acceptable, and well tolerated for knee osteoarthritis. Participants valued its convenience and non-pharmacological nature. These findings support a fully powered trial to determine whether this scalable approach improves pain and function and broadens access to care.

title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture.
DESIGN: Systematic review.
DATA SOURCES: Web of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Human genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: 19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: COL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.

title: Updates on Low Energy Availability in Athletes: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and the Female or Male Athlete Triad.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This paper evaluates the latest literature on low energy availability (LEA) in athletes, which is the basis for the clinical conditions known as the Female Athlete Triad, Male Athlete Triad, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). It explores how these different conditions are related, and how the clinician can approach screening, diagnosis, and management of LEA in athletes.
RECENT FINDINGS: Within the past five years the Male Athlete Triad Consensus Statements were published in 2021, expanding upon knowledge regarding LEA in the Female Athlete Triad and applying this to the male population. Additionally, there has been an important update to the REDs model and a new clinical assessment tool (CAT2) published in 2023. This is based on new research into the different physiologic and psychologic sequelae of LEA. This has sparked additional discussion regarding the diagnosis, management, and prevention of LEA. The consequences of LEA can be severe, and can affect multiple different organ systems. Treatment should ideally involve a multidisciplinary team consisting of a physician, dietitian, and mental health provider, but may also include additional professionals such as athletic trainers, physical therapists, physiologists, other medical specialists, or other members of the athlete support system (including family and coaches). The mainstay of management remains optimizing energy availability (EA) through improving macro and micronutrient intake, and also requires addressing some of the more common sequelae of LEA. Prevention largely focuses on educational efforts and fostering healthy environments, particularly when discussing weight, body composition, and performance.

title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points.
METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles.
RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions.
CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

title: Health, Risk and Adaptation in Extreme Open Water Swimming: A Qualitative Study of Channel Swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Participation in extreme open water swimming, including channel swimming, has increased markedly, yet health research has focused largely on quantifying risks rather than understanding athletes' lived experiences. This study explored how experienced channel swimmers perceive health issues, prevention strategies, and recovery across preparation, performance, and post-swim phases.
METHODS: A qualitative, interpretive study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 30 swimmers who had completed at least two Oceans Seven channel swims. The study was conducted between April and September 2021. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Themes were developed inductively to capture physical, psychological, and management-related aspects of health.
RESULTS: Three interconnected themes were identified: (1) physical and physiological lived experience, (2) psychological and cognitive journey, and (3) proactive and reactive management. Pain, injury, and hypothermia were widely normalised as inherent to the sport, and chronic musculoskeletal problems were routinely managed rather than avoided. Notably, swimmers located maximum danger within the swim itself, while several of the most serious consequences-including swimming-induced pulmonary edema, pneumonia, and prolonged neurological symptoms-emerged only after completion. Psychological challenges included in-swim cognitive impairment, recognised only retrospectively, and post-swim emotional lows linked to the removal of a defining goal rather than to failure. Health management relied heavily on experiential knowledge, with swimmers using individualised strategies for preparation, real-time decision-making, and recovery. Recovery was viewed as an active, holistic process and a critical learning phase informing future swims.
CONCLUSIONS: Health in channel swimming is understood by athletes as a dynamic, adaptive process shaped by experience and community norms. These findings informed the development of TIDE (Training and Resilience, Intensity and Stress, Decision-making and Coping, Evolution and Feedback), a non-linear framework conceptualising marathon swimming as a continuous feedback loop in which each swim shapes preparation for the next. TIDE offers clinicians, coaches, and event organisers a framework for identifying, where an athlete's adaptive cycle is overwhelmed or temporarily disrupted, and provides a basis for formalising the experiential knowledge that currently protects only the most experienced swimmers as participation continues to grow.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.
