title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.

title: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications.
abstract: Wearable sensors enable continuous acquisition of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals during exercise, providing data to support sports performance assessment, training regulation, fatigue monitoring, and rehabilitation interventions. However, signal reliability and multidimensional data analysis under complex motion conditions remain constrained by device functionality. Conductive composites can improve sensor flexibility, interfacial conformability, and signal acquisition performance, while artificial intelligence (AI) enables movement pattern recognition, state assessment, and outcome prediction from complex data. Their integration is advancing wearable systems toward multimodal sensing and intelligent analysis. Guided by application needs in sports, this review summarizes emerging applications of wearable sensing technologies enabled by conductive composites and AI. First, the relevance to sports science and the data characteristics of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals are introduced. The functional characteristics, representative applications, and major limitations of conductive polymer, carbon-based, MXene, and hydrogel composites are then summarized. Regarding algorithms, the fundamental principles of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) are discussed, with comparisons of their capabilities in feature extraction, temporal modeling, and multisource data analysis, as well as their input data requirements. On this basis, advances in the application of these systems to sports performance and sport-specific movement monitoring, exercise-induced fatigue monitoring and assessment, sports injury identification and evaluation, and intelligent monitoring of sports rehabilitation are reviewed followed by a discussion of current challenges and future directions. Through the coordinated integration of material design, signal acquisition, and intelligent analysis, wearable systems are expected to enable continuous, reliable, and individualized assessment of exercise-related states, with further applications in real-time feedback, risk alerts, and training decision support, providing a technological foundation for scientifically informed training, sports rehabilitation, and individual health management.

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

title: Eating Behavior, Body Appreciation, and Sleep Quality in Italian Blind Baseball Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Survey.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Visual impairment is associated with poor sleep quality, psychological distress, and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. Adapted sports, such as blind baseball (BXC), may help promote healthy lifestyles and overall well-being. However, evidence regarding eating behavior, sleep quality, body appreciation, and lifestyle habits among regular BXC players remains scarce. This cross-sectional study provides an exploratory multidimensional characterization of these domains in competitive Italian BXC athletes according to sport participation and visual impairment characteristics, comparing findings descriptively with normative data from the Italian general population. Methods: Fifty-three competitive Italian BXC players (mean age 39.3 ± 13.1 years; representing a response rate of 49.1% of the national league) completed an anonymous online survey assessing eating behavior (Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire, AEBQ), body appreciation (Body Appreciation Scale-2, BAS-2), sleep quality (Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, B-PSQI), and lifestyle habits. Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, reporting medians, interquartile ranges, effect sizes (rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence intervals. Results: BXC athletes demonstrated BMI, sleep quality, eating behavior, and body appreciation profiles comparable to those of the Italian general population. BAS-2 scores were high (3.7-3.8), while B-PSQI scores (4.0-5.6) and the proportion of poor sleepers (~40%) remained within normative ranges despite visual impairment. Eating behavior showed no significant dysregulation. However, in exploratory subgroup analyses, multisport athletes displayed lower Satiety Responsiveness than BXC-only athletes (2.30 ± 0.79 vs. 2.78 ± 0.71; p = 0.02), poorer sleep quality (B-PSQI: 6.05 ± 3.12 vs. 4.70 ± 3.73; p = 0.05), and a higher prevalence of poor sleep (55.0% vs. 30.3%). Athletes with acquired visual impairment showed higher Emotional Overeating and Emotional Undereating scores than those with congenital impairment, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: BXC athletes displayed an overall favorable lifestyle profile. Though the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, these exploratory findings indicate that participation in BXC is compatible with healthy lifestyle habits and positive body appreciation, hence supporting adapted team sports as an inclusive framework for multidimensional health promotion. Future studies using objective physiological assessments and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify dose-response relationships and long-term health outcomes.

title: Global Positioning System-Derived Match Demands and Their Association With On-Field Technical Performance in Elite Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) Athletes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study sought to determine the associations between global positioning system-derived match demands and technical performance in elite Australian Football League Women's athletes.
METHODS: Global positioning system match demands (total distance, speed, acceleration, high-intensity running [>19 km·h-1], very high-intensity running [>21 km·h-1], sprint distances [>24 km·h-1]) were measured with Catapult Vector S7 global positioning system units during the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes for each game were considered technical performance outcomes. Linear mixed effects regression models examined associations between match demands and technical performance, adjusting for season, ground location, and playing position.
RESULTS: Five hundred sixty-six player match profiles from 32 athletes across the 2 seasons were analyzed. Ranking points were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .29 [95% CI .22-.40]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.15]), and acceleration (R2 = .09 [.00-.23]). Best and fairest votes were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .23 [.17-.34]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.11]), acceleration (R2 = .05 [.00-.17]), and very high-intensity running distance per minute (R2 = .00 [.00-.13]).
CONCLUSIONS: Total distance, speed, acceleration, and very high-intensity running distance per minute were associated with Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes across Australian Football League Women's seasons 2023 and 2024. This suggests that athletes who cover greater total distances and achieve higher average acceleration get more opportunities to be involved in match-play and demonstrate higher levels of technical performance.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient.
METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only.
RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses.
CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

title: Musculoskeletal injury patterns and factors associated with anatomical injury location among surveyed padel players in Saudi Arabia: A cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundPadel is a growing sport in Saudi Arabia; however, data on related musculoskeletal injuries and associated factors are limited. The increasing number of players highlights the importance of understanding padel-related injury patterns and their associated characteristics.ObjectiveTo describe self-reported musculoskeletal injury patterns among surveyed padel players in Saudi Arabia and examine player-, exposure-, equipment-, and injury-related characteristics associated with anatomical injury location among reported injury cases.MethodA cross-sectional study was conducted using a self-administered questionnaire distributed through convenience and snowball sampling to padel players in Saudi Arabia between February and March 2025. The questionnaire collected information on demographic characteristics, playing exposure, equipment characteristics, injury history, and injury-related characteristics.ResultsA total of 600 padel players were included in the analysis, of whom 301 reported at least one padel-related musculoskeletal injury, corresponding to 50.2% of the surveyed sample, with 513 reported injury cases. Upper-quadrant injuries were the most frequently reported (44.1%), followed by foot/ankle (22.4%), spine (18.5%), and knee injuries (15.0%). In multivariable GEE analyses of reported injury observations, weekly playing hours were associated with foot/ankle and knee injury classification. Other significant associations with anatomical injury classification involved ADL limitation, pain severity, recovery duration, recurrence, sex, padel education, and racket hardness, with patterns varying by anatomical location.ConclusionThese findings characterize self-reported musculoskeletal injury patterns among surveyed padel players and identify characteristics associated with anatomical injury location. Prospective studies are needed to determine factors associated with subsequent injury occurrence and to inform targeted preventive strategies.

title: More than a shot: function over pain with tele-supervised resistance exercise added to hyaluronic acid injection in knee osteoarthritis, a randomized add-on trial.
abstract: Exercise is central to knee osteoarthritis (KOA) care, and intra-articular hyaluronic acid (IAHA) is often used as an adjunct, yet access to supervised exercise after injection is limited. Whether adding tele-supervised resistance band exercise (TSBE) improves outcomes beyond IAHA alone is unclear. Eighty adults with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 1-3 KOA who had not responded adequately to conservative care received a single IAHA injection and were allocated to a 12-week TSBE or standard education without supervised exercise. The between-group difference in Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total change favoured TSBE (-5 points, 95% CI - 9.86 to -0.13; p = .044). TSBE also favoured WOMAC physical function (-4.88, 95% CI - 8.28 to -1.47), 30-second sit-to-stand (+3.79 repetitions, 95% CI 2.80 to 4.79), and timed up-and-go (-1.87 s, 95% CI - 2.34 to -1.41), but not VAS pain (-0.38, 95% CI - 1.00 to 0.25). Adding TSBE to IAHA improved function and mobility, with no additional reduction in pain.

title: Adjustment of the Anteroposterior Center-of-Pressure Position Reduces Asymmetrical Knee Loading During Double-Leg Squatting After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract: Asymmetrical knee extension moments (KEMs) are associated with poor clinical outcomes following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. However, effective corrective methods remain limited. Thirty-four individuals (144.1 [60.2] d postanterior cruciate ligament reconstruction) performed 12 sets of 5 squats with visual feedback to maintain a symmetrical anteroposterior center-of-pressure position. Limb symmetry indices were calculated for KEM, vertical ground reaction force, and knee-to-support moment ratio (knee moment divided by the sum of hip, knee, and ankle extension moments). A mixed-model analysis of variance examined the effects of group (asymmetry: baseline KEM limb symmetry indices < 90%; symmetry: ≥90%) and time (baseline, post-biofeedback). Biomechanical changes were observed primarily within the asymmetry group (21 participants), which showed increases in limb symmetry indices for KEM (73.0% [10.5%] vs 85.4% [15.5%], P < .001), knee-to-support moment ratio (81.0% [16.7%] vs 87.4% [14.8%], P = .006), and vertical ground reaction force (90.5% [7.1%] vs 96.3% [8.6%], P = .003). Notably, these differences were primarily driven by changes in the uninvolved limb rather than the involved limb. No significant changes were observed in the symmetry group. While biofeedback of the anteroposterior center-of-pressure position reduced asymmetrical knee loading, further strategies are required to specifically elicit changes in the involved limb.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

title: Body Mass, Strength, Power, and Endurance Variations Across an Entire Season in Male Basketball Players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to analyze changes in body mass, upper- and lower-boy strength, vertical jump performance, and endurance capacity in senior semiprofessional basketball players across 4 different time points (TPs) during the season.
METHODS: Fifteen male basketball players (n = 15; age: 23.4 [3.4] y; height: 1.9 [0.1] m) volunteered to participate in this study. Participants were tested for body mass, 1-repetition maximum in the squat and bench press exercises, countermovement jump (CMJ) and loaded CMJ, and 30-15 intermittent fitness test.
RESULTS: Significant increases were observed in absolute and relative 1-repetition maximum in the squat (P < .03; effect size [ES]: moderate to large) from TP1 to TP2, TP3, and TP4. Regarding CMJ, greater jump heights were observed at TP2 and TP4 when compared with TP3 (P < .015; ES: small). In the loaded CMJ (ES: moderate), loads were significantly greater at TP2, TP3, and TP4 compared with TP1 (P < .009; ES: moderate). Conversely, 30-15 intermittent fitness test measures showed small but nonsignificant increments (P < .086; ES: small).
CONCLUSIONS: Lower-body strength and power measures improved during the preseason in male basketball players, with these athletes being able to retain strength levels across the in-season period, despite the congested competitive schedule. In contrast, CMJ performance did not change during the preseason but appeared to be negatively affected during the most competition-dense phase of the season (ie, TP3). Finally, endurance capacity and body mass remained relatively stable from the beginning of the preseason until the end of the season.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Different osteoarthritis progression rates within early-stage knee osteoarthritis: a retrospective cohort study using machine learning cluster analysis from the osteoarthritis initiative database.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disease with varying progression rates among patients within the same severity grade. This study aimed to identify clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes among knees with baseline Kellgren and Lawrence (KL) grade 2 osteoarthritis and to compare their 4-year radiographic progression patterns using baseline radiographic features, lifetime exercise patterns, and demographic characteristics.
METHODS: Data of patients with baseline KL grade 2 from the Osteoarthritis Initiative database were retrieved. Unsupervised clustering was performed using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) for dimensionality reduction, followed by hierarchical density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (HDBSCAN) to identify distinct subgroups. The proportion of knees progressing to KL grade ≥ 3 within 4 years was compared between subgroups, followed by a survival analysis until knee replacement or progression to KL grade 4.
RESULTS: A total of 1997 knees with a mean follow-up of 103.3 months (maximum, 108 months) were included. A total of seven subgroups were identified and classified into accelerated osteoarthritis progression (AOP) group and slow osteoarthritis progression (SOP) group according to whether their 4-year KL grade progression proportions were above or below the training-set average. In a supportive long-term survival analysis, the AOP group also showed significantly earlier progression to knee replacement or KL grade 4 than the SOP group (training set, P < 0.001; test set, P = 0.049), although the absolute difference in mean survival time was modest (8.3 versus 8.5 years in the training set; 8.4 versus 8.6 years in the test set). The AOP group was characterized mainly by lateral joint space narrowing (JSN) and medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, whereas the SOP group was characterized by medial JSN without subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant patterns without JSN, or chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns; these differences were statistically significant across clusters.
CONCLUSIONS: Within baseline KL grade 2 knees, clinically interpretable radiographic phenotypes, including lateral JSN, medial JSN with subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte-dominant changes without JSN, and chondrocalcinosis-dominant patterns, were associated with different 4-year KL grade progression rates. These findings support viewing KL grade 2 knee OA as a heterogeneous radiographic stage that may be further stratified into phenotype-based subgroups with different short-term radiographic prognoses.

title: Pelvic floor knowledge and unhealthy habits related in female athletes: a cross-sectional study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To describe pelvic floor (PF)-related knowledge and unhealthy habits among female athletes, and to examine their associations with PF dysfunction (PFD) symptoms, sports characteristics, academic level and help seeking attitudes.
METHODS: A total of 538 female athletes (36.7 ± 11.3 years) completed an anonymous online questionnaire covering age, academic level, sports experience, unhealthy PF-related habits, PFD symptoms, professional healthcare-seeking attitude and knowledge about urinary incontinence (UI), anorectal incontinence (ARI), pelvic organ prolapse (POP) and female sexual dysfunction (FSD). Adequate knowledge was considered as ≥70% correct responses.
RESULTS: Female athletes demonstrated adequate knowledge regarding UI, ARI and POP, but insufficient knowledge about FSD (52.6%). Several PFD symptoms were associated with lower knowledge levels and a higher number of unhealthy habits compared with athletes without these symptoms (p<0.05). Younger athletes showed lower knowledge about ARI (p=0.033) and POP (p=0.003), while older athletes showed lower knowledge about FSD (p<0.001). Athletes who rejected professional healthcare showed lower knowledge across all PFD domains (p<0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Female athletes reporting symptoms suggestive of PFD showed lower levels of knowledge and a higher number of unhealthy PF habits compared with those without symptoms. Although athletes generally demonstrated an appropriate level of knowledge regarding PFD, important gaps were observed in the FSD domain and in unhealthy toileting and sport-related habits, particularly among athletes without university studies. Differences in knowledge were also observed according to age and healthcare-seeking attitudes, highlighting areas that may be considered in future educational initiatives.

title: Case Study Insights Into Female World-Class and Elite Athletes' Training and Physiology.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This article offers a structured overview of published case studies involving elite and world-class female Olympic athletes, highlighting the unique insights these studies provide into training characteristics, physiology, performance, and female-specific factors.
METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for peer-reviewed case studies involving tiers 4 to 5 female Olympic athletes reporting individual-level data on training, physiological, and/or performance characteristics.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight studies describing 54 elite and world-class female athletes from 18 countries and 19 Olympic sports met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were published after 2017 (68%), originated from Europe (58%), and involved endurance sports (81%). Fifteen studies examined long-term athlete development, with observation periods ranging from 4 to 26 years. Fourteen studies reported annual training and physiological characteristics across 10 sports including training volume, intensity distribution, periodization, and physiological profiling. Four studies examined altitude training, 8 addressed competition demands, tapering, and precompetition strategies, and 8 focused on female-specific physiology, health, and performance, including energy availability, menstrual function, hormonal cycle monitoring and pregnancy, and postpartum return to sport.
CONCLUSION: Case studies provide unique athlete-centered insights into the complex interactions between training, physiology, health, and performance in elite female athletes. Collectively, they demonstrate that pathways to world-class performance are highly individualized, while generating hypotheses that complement group-based research. Future case studies should prioritize underrepresented sports, geographical regions, and female-specific topics to expand the diversity of performance environments and athlete populations represented in the literature.

title: "Why wouldn't you?": the co-design and feasibility of a neck exercise training programme (NExT-TaCKLE) to reduce head acceleration events in men's academy rugby league.
abstract: This qualitative study aimed to co-design and explore the feasibility, barriers and facilitators of a neck-exercise training intervention aiming to reduce head acceleration events (HAEs) in men's academy rugby league. A steering group of researchers and practitioners from five academy rugby league teams co-designed a neck-training programme (Neck Exercise Training - Tackle and Contact Kinematics, Load, Exposure (NExT-TaCKLE) programme). The NExT-TaCKLE programme was designed to give performance and medical practitioners exercises catering to different equipment availability; target neck musculature across flexion, extension, bilateral flexion and rotation; and progress from movement competency to perturbation-focused training blocks. The NExT-TacCKLE programme was trialled for a 6-week period in three teams. Semistructured interviews were completed with a practitioner and player from each team to determine the feasibility of NExT-TacCKLE, including barriers and facilitators to implementation. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse the interview data and generate themes. Data were then revisited and mapped to feasibility areas of interest and the capability, opportunity and motivation model for behaviour change. Eight themes were generated during the reflexive thematic analysis. The programme showed good acceptability and demand; however, the implementation, integration and practicality were feasibility areas where the programme could be improved. Key barriers (eg, equipment, coach-to-athlete ratio, practitioner experience) and facilitators (eg, belief in the intervention effectiveness, perceived simple integration into existing setups) were identified. Working with practitioners, the NExT-TaCKLE programme was developed for implementation with academy rugby league players. This study can help inform future development of the NExT-TaCKLE and other neck-training programmes, as well as other injury prevention and implementation strategies. Future research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of the programme to reduce HAEs.

title: Integrated Decision-Making Under Uncertainty in High-Performance Sport Support Systems.
abstract: Greater expertise, more data, and increased collaboration do not necessarily improve decisions in high-performance sport. Support systems must connect evidence and professional judgement to action under time pressure, uncertainty, and competing priorities. This narrative review draws on targeted database and citation searches to synthesize literature on performance support, team functioning, leadership, sport science, and decision science. The proposed framework combines established decision principles with qualitative triage and selective integration. Urgency, uncertainty, risk and consequences, reversibility, interdisciplinary interdependence, and stakeholder differences guide the choice between discipline-led decisions, consultation or coordinated input, and integrated decision-making. Five interdependent functions organize integrated work: framing the problem and decision; identifying contributors and governance; interpreting information and generating options; committing to and communicating a course of action; and acting, monitoring, and learning. Governance distinguishes information provision, recommendations, final authority, and implementation responsibility, with referral or escalation available from any working mode. Athlete values and decision rights shape the process, including shared decision-making and consent where required. Coaches help translate recommendations into feasible training and competition plans. Scientific reasoning, applied inquiry, innovation, and integrative leadership support these functions. Hypothetical examples address return to sport, training modification, and technology adoption. The framework remains conceptual, and evaluation should examine content validity, usability, triage consistency, implementation burden, and decision processes before assessing health and performance effects. Decision quality should be judged against the information and uncertainty present when decisions were made.

title: Using double-bundle Achilles tendon-bone allograft for reconstruction of compound loss of lateral malleolus and lateral ankle ligaments: A rare case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Composite defects of the lateral ankle, involving bone loss, ligament disruption, and soft tissue compromise, cause profound mechanical instability and are difficult to reconstruct with techniques that address bone or ligaments alone.
PATIENT CONCERNS: We report a 26-year-old woman who presented with progressive right ankle pain, recurrent giving-way, and peroneal tendon subluxation 7 years after a high-energy crush injury that required flap coverage.
DIAGNOSES: Lateral malleolar loss with a distal fibular bony defect measuring approximately 5 × 3 × 2 cm and chronic varus instability; complete anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) rupture; and peroneal tendon dislocation were confirmed by stress radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging.
INTERVENTIONS: Single-stage reconstruction with a cryopreserved Achilles tendon-bone allograft. The calcaneal bone block was contoured and fixed to the fibular stump with a 4.5-mm cannulated screw to reconstitute the lateral malleolus. The tendon was split into 2 bundles (7 mm × 30 mm for the ATFL and 7 mm × 40 mm for the CFL) for anatomic ATFL and CFL reconstruction and secured with interference screws at the talar and calcaneal footprints. The peroneal tendons were reduced after bony restoration. Postoperative rehabilitation used an Aircast® brace with non-weight-bearing ambulation for the first 3 weeks, partial weight-bearing from week 3, full weight-bearing by week 6, and brace discontinuation at week 12.
OUTCOMES: At the final follow-up of 16 months, the patient ambulated pain-free with a stable ankle. Radiographs demonstrated successful incorporation of the bone allograft, and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed intact ATFL/CFL grafts with maintained peroneal tendon reduction. Functional scores were Karlsson-Peterson 87 and American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society ankle-hindfoot 90.
LESSONS: A double-bundle Achilles tendon-bone allograft enables simultaneous reconstruction of lateral malleolar bone and lateral ligaments, avoiding donor-site morbidity and achieving durable stability in complex, previously reconstructed ankles. This approach should be considered when both osseous and ligamentous deficits coexist.

title: Maximum-Effort Jumping Exposes the Achilles Tendon to High Strain and Indicates Potential Overload in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract: Plyometric exercise is a fundamental component of many sport disciplines and may overload the Achilles tendon (AT) by subjecting it to high strain magnitudes. AT strain profiles were investigated during countermovement, drop, hurdle, and horizontal single-leg jumps - common plyometric exercises - in order to assess exercise-induced AT loading. This was done by measuring AT elongation during the jumps using reflective markers on the skin to reconstruct the AT path, while the myotendinous junction of the gastrocnemius medialis was recorded using ultrasound in 18 adolescent athletes. Electromyographic (EMG) activity of the tibialis anterior, soleus, gastrocnemius medialis and lateralis muscles, kinematics, and ground reaction forces were also measured. Although the maximum resultant ankle joint moment differed significantly between the investigated jumps, maximum AT strain and EMG activity of the triceps surae muscles were invariant between jump types. On average, the maximum AT strains ranged from 9.0% to 10.7%, and the EMG activity ranged from 0.96 to 1.43 times the maximum EMG activity achieved during a maximum voluntary fixed-end plantar flexion contraction, across the jumps. The consistently high AT strain magnitudes across the investigated jumps highlight the substantial mechanical demand placed on the AT during maximum-effort jumping tasks, which exceed the reported effective strain range for tendon adaptation. The frequent application of plyometric exercises involving such high-magnitude strains in training practice may contribute to AT overload in adolescent athletes.

title: Editorial Commentary: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Requires the Right Patient, the Right Dose, and the Right Time.
abstract: Quadriceps weakness is a persistent challenge after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. When used as an adjunct to rehabilitation, neuromuscular electrical stimulation can aid in quadriceps strength recovery. However, optimizing the clinical application of neuromuscular electrical stimulation requires consideration of the right patient, the right dose, and the right time. Volitional activation failure can limit adequate voluntary loading of the quadriceps, particularly in the early postoperative period. Although the evidence supports early neuromuscular electrical stimulation use when activation deficits are most pronounced, treatment should be guided by resolution of underlying impairments rather than postoperative time alone.

title: Being treated as more than a diagnosis: A qualitative interview study exploring patients' experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance in the management of tendinopathy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tendinopathy rehabilitation often involves exercise therapy and patient education. However, limited research has explored how patients experience and assign meaning to the guidance through which such care is delivered.
OBJECTIVES: This study aims to explore how adults with tendinopathy experience and make sense of physiotherapeutic guidance in clinical practice.
STUDY DESIGN: This qualitative study adopted a hermeneutic approach and employed semi-structured interviews with 10 patients receiving treatment for tendinopathy across various anatomical regions to explore their experiences of physiotherapeutic guidance throughout treatment.
RESULTS: From the patients' responses, two major themes were identified: "Meaningful guidance is built through trust, recognition, and individualisation" and "Purposeful guidance helps patients understand and manage the condition". Three sub-themes surfaced within each theme, and similar topics were identified among the patients' responses.
CONCLUSIONS: Physiotherapeutic guidance appears to be meaningful when it integrates relational and functional processes. While trust, recognition, and individualisation support patients' engagement, clear explanations and structured guidance facilitate understanding and self-management in daily life.

title: Delayed Extensor Apparatus Reconstruction for Post-Burn Digital Extension Loss in a Pediatric Patient.
abstract: Late sequelae of pediatric hand burns may include occult damage to the digital extensor apparatus beneath healed scar tissue. The digital extensor apparatus is a complex anatomical system composed of interconnected components that function together to produce coordinated finger extension at interphalangeal joints. Injury to this system may remain clinically unrecognized during acute burn management and present later as isolated extension loss despite preserved joint suppleness. We report the case of a 10-year-old girl who presented 2 years after a flame burn involving the dorsum of the left hand with inability to actively extend the index and middle fingers. Clinical examination demonstrated absent active extension at the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, whereas passive motion, sensation, and vascularity were preserved. Overlying skin was supple, though scarred and variably pigmented. Radiographs demonstrated mild proximal interphalangeal joint subluxation of the middle finger without other osseous abnormality. Surgical exploration revealed loss of functional continuity of the digital extensor apparatus distally. Delayed reconstruction was performed using an ipsilateral palmaris longus tendon graft to restore coordinated extension. Temporary axial K-wire immobilization was maintained for 2 weeks, followed by structured rehabilitation. At final follow-up, the patient achieved approximately 80% recovery of active extension, enabling writing and functional grasp. This case underscores the importance of early recognition of occult extensor apparatus damage following pediatric hand burns to prevent functional disability. However, delayed reconstruction can still yield meaningful functional recovery when joint mobility and neurovascular integrity are preserved.

title: Sports-related peripheral neuropathies in athletes: mechanisms, imaging evaluation, and sport-specific patterns.
abstract: Peripheral neuropathy in athletes is increasingly recognized as a significant source of morbidity, with injury patterns varying according to the biomechanical demands of specific sports. Although peripheral nerve disorders in athletes may result from acute trauma, they more commonly arise from chronic, repetitive mechanical stress inherent to athletic activity. Despite their frequency, they frequently remain underdiagnosed, as clinical manifestations often overlap with other musculoskeletal disorders. Mechanisms of injury include compression, traction, laceration, ischemia, and repetitive microtrauma. Distinct athletic modalities are associated with characteristic neuropathies reflecting sport-specific kinematics and loading patterns. Awareness of these biomechanical factors and recognition of typical clinical presentations are essential for accurate assessment of athletes with suspected nerve injury. Diagnostic evaluation frequently requires advanced imaging modalities, particularly magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) and high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS), which enable detailed structural assessment of peripheral nerves and detection of secondary imaging findings. Electrodiagnostic studies may provide complementary functional information in selected cases. Early and precise diagnosis is critical to guide management, facilitate safe return to sport, and prevent long-term functional deficits. While most nerve disorders respond to conservative treatment, severe, progressive, or refractory cases may warrant surgical intervention to restore function and enable return to play (RTP). This review examines mechanisms of injury, clinical evaluation, classification systems, imaging findings, and sport-specific patterns of peripheral nerve injury across diverse athletic disciplines.

title: Player, Coach, and Performance Staff Perceptions of, Experiences with, and Preferences for Nutrition Services Within Rugby: An Implementation‑Focused Qualitative Exploration.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: To explore how players, performance staff, and dietitians perceive, experience, and prefer nutrition services within professional rugby, a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, guided by an implementation science lens (Integrated Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services, i-PARIHS), was conducted.
METHODS: Purposeful sampling was used to recruit 27 participants (13 professional players, 5 dietitians, 1 coach, 3 strength and conditioning coaches, 3 physiotherapists, 2 high-performance managers) from an Australian professional rugby organisation. Interviews were conducted online between April 2024 and July 2025, transcribed, inductively coded, and thematically analysed with iterative verification by multiple researchers. Analysis was completed to support understanding of factors that may influence implementation, including the i-PARIHS constructs of innovation, recipients, and context.
RESULTS: Three inter-related themes were generated. (1) Organisational value and role clarity determined dietitians' visibility, influence, and the credibility of nutrition messaging; when nutrition was not championed by leadership and performance staff, advice was fragmented and dietitians' contribution was reduced to narrow, "tangible" metrics. (2) Food practices were the primary vehicle through which nutrition services were enacted, including menu planning, food provision, shared meals, and food-literacy support; nutrition service gaps were most evident in women's, pathway, and rehabilitation contexts and for athletes experiencing food insecurity. (3) Limited resourcing constrained proactive delivery, relationship-building, and long-term planning, forcing reactive practice and uneven access across programs.
CONCLUSIONS: Nutrition was widely regarded as foundational to growth, preparation, recovery, broader training adaptation, and athlete well-being in rugby, yet current delivery models underperform due to undervaluation, blurred responsibilities, and insufficient staffing and food-system support. Findings suggest elevating dietetics to fully integrated, full-time roles and embedding equitable food-centred provision and food-literacy interventions are necessary to improve consistency, uptake, and athlete outcomes, and to reduce avoidable inequities between squads nationally.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears in the anterior cruciate ligament-injured knee: Current concepts.
abstract: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears (LMPRTs) compromise load transmission and secondary stability in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-injured knee and may be missed on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This narrative current-concepts review addresses incidence, risk factors, biomechanics, diagnosis, classification, treatment, and outcomes, while distinguishing root tears from lateral meniscal oblique radial tears (LMORTs). Primary ACL reconstruction (ACLR) cohorts report LMPRT frequencies of 7.1%, 10.0%, and 12.2%; a mixed primary/revision cohort reports 6.6% and selected revision cohorts report 20.5% and 40.7%. These study-specific estimates differ in lesion definition and ascertainment. Contact injury, concomitant medial meniscal pathology, and increased lateral posterior tibial slope are recurring associations. Individual MRI signs have limited sensitivity; combined assessment and arthroscopic inspection and probing support diagnosis. LaPrade et al. describe root-tear morphology, Forkel and Petersen additionally consider meniscofemoral ligament integrity, and LMORT typing describes posterior-horn oblique radial tears. The systems overlap for near-root lesions and are descriptive frameworks rather than validated treatment algorithms. Selected stable lesions may be observed; repairable unstable lesions are generally treated with footprint fixation or side-to-side repair, according to anatomy and tissue quality. Repair with ACLRn is associated with improved patient-reported outcomes and high complete-or-partial healing proportions in selected series. Clinical improvement in ACL graft survivorship has not been demonstrated. Heterogeneous definitions, predominantly lower-level evidence, variable rehabilitation, and limited long-term comparative data, constrain conclusions about cartilage preservation and optimal treatment.

title: A mechanically active microneedle platform integrated with engineered exosomes for enhanced tendon-bone regeneration.
abstract: Functional regeneration of the tendon-bone interface remains a major challenge because early healing is constrained by an adverse inflammatory microenvironment and insufficient mechanical cues. Here, we developed a mechano-regenerative strategy that combines YAP-primed engineered exosomes with localized biomaterial-based delivery and active mechanical stimulation. Exosomes derived from a YAP agonist (PY-60) preconditioned TDSCs (P-Exo) showed enhanced uptake and promoted the osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, accompanied by activation of YAP-associated signaling and PI3K-Akt-related pathways. To improve local retention, P-Exo were incorporated into a ROS-responsive adhesive hydrogel, which accelerated fibrocartilage formation, bone ingrowth, and biomechanical restoration in a rabbit tendon-bone healing model. To address more complex repair conditions, we engineered a three-layer self-contracting microneedle platform for deep-tissue delivery of P-Exo with concurrent active mechanical stimulation. In an infected rat rotator cuff model, this system reduced bacterial burden and oxidative stress, promoted a reparative macrophage polarization and angiogenesis, and improved tendon-bone structural regeneration, biomechanical strength, and functional recovery. Together, these findings support a therapeutic framework in which engineered exosome signaling and active mechanoregulation act in concert to enhance tendon-bone repair.

title: High Survival and Continued Sports Participation After Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Athletes With and Without Lateral Rim Dysplasia With Minimum 4.5-Year Follow-Up.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To quantify the outcomes, including sporting capability, of hip arthroscopy (HA) in athletes for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) in the presence of concomitant lateral rim dysplasia (LR-Dysplasia) compared with a matched athletic control group.
METHODS: Athletes undergoing unilateral primary HA for FAI with or without LR-Dysplasia between January 2009 and May 2020 were considered. All athletes with a lateral center-edge angle of <25° on anteroposterior view were matched to those with normal overcoverage (lateral center-edge angle >30°). Patients were contacted a minimum of 4.5 years after the procedure. Outcomes included survival (avoidance of total hip replacement), revision HA, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) consisting of the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity score, 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Substantial clinical benefit thresholds were determined for each PROM, and the proportion of cases achieving substantial clinical benefit was compared between groups. Finally, the ability to continue to play sports and satisfaction were determined.
RESULTS: Forty-eight patients with LR-Dysplasia were matched to 97 controls with a mean follow-up of 72 ± 19 months (54-120 months). At follow-up, survival was 100% in the LR-Dysplasia group versus 99% in controls. The revision HA rates were 6% in LR-Dysplasia patients and 9% in controls. Both groups showed significant improvements in PROMs. In the LR-Dysplasia group, mHHS improved from 82 to 100 (P < .001), UCLA from 8 to 9 (P = .114), SF-36 from 74 to 87 (P = .002), and WOMAC from 15 to 2 (P < .001). In the control group, mHHS improved from 82 to 96 (P < .001), UCLA from 7 to 10 (P = .003), SF-36 from 72 to 89 (P < .001), and WOMAC from 17 to 4 (P = .005). Between-group comparisons showed no significant differences in pre- or postoperative mHHS (P = .498; P = .183), UCLA (P = .684; P = .388), SF-36 (P = .487; P = .602), or WOMAC (P = .814; P = .390). Substantial clinical benefit was achieved by most patients for each PROM and similar between groups (P > .05 for all). No significant differences were observed between groups in PROMs or overall satisfaction with surgery (P > .05 for all). Sports participation at 5 years was 84% in the LR-Dysplasia group and 90% in controls (P = .103).
CONCLUSIONS: In the absence of arthritic changes, athletes treated with arthroscopy for FAI where LR-Dysplasia is present showed high survival rates and improved pain and function. Furthermore, most athletes can maintain their preoperative levels of sport. Importantly, the outcomes observed in this specific patient cohort are comparable to those seen in athletes with normal acetabular coverage, indicating that the presence of LR-Dysplasia does not compromise the effectiveness of arthroscopic intervention for FAI in athletes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.

title: Effect of subtendon-specific loading on strain heterogeneity in the rat Achilles tendon across gaits: A finite element study.
abstract: The Achilles tendon is comprised of three subtendons connecting to the soleus and the lateral and medial gastrocnemius muscles. These subtendons transmit load partly independently, resulting in non-uniform deformation of the tendon. Most previous computational models treating the tendon as a single homogeneous structure cannot capture the heterogeneous mechanics of the tendon. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the strain heterogeneity arising from subtendinous physiological gait loading in an anatomically detailed FE model of the rat Achilles tendon. To achieve this, phase-contrast enhanced synchrotron X-ray tomography images of rat Achilles tendons were segmented to identify the subtendon geometry and fiber distribution. Subtendon-specific experimental forces were obtained from the literature for walking, trotting, and galloping. The effect of subtendon-specific loading was investigated by comparing it to uniform loading, in which the same total force was applied to the whole proximal cross-section without distinguishing the subtendons. The resulting subtendon elongations, principal strains, shear stresses, and fluid velocities were analyzed to understand the effect of the loading scheme for various gait conditions. The results show that subtendon-specific loading substantially affected the tendon's mechanical behavior. It reproduced the differential subtendon elongation of a healthy tendon, with medial gastrocnemius elongation up to 27% higher and soleus elongation up to 29% lower than under uniform loading. Subtendinous loading also produced greater strain heterogeneity, with a maximum principal strain of 16% higher than with uniform loading, localized shear stress concentrations at the subtendon interfaces, and higher fluid velocities in the gastrocnemius compartments. Capturing these heterogeneous strain distributions is important for future mechanobiological predictions of tendon adaptation, injury, and healing.

title: Altered mechanical and vascular responses of the Achilles tendon to acute loading in Kendo athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to elucidate acute, bilateral Achilles tendon (AT) responses to high-intensity single-leg hopping in Kendo athletes and healthy controls.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty Kendo athletes and 20 sedentary controls performed a single-leg hopping task. Ultrasound imaging assessed AT anteroposterior diameter (APD), shear wave velocity (SWV), and intratendinous vessel count before (PRE), immediately after (POST), and 5-min post-exercise (POST5).
RESULTS: Following exercise, Kendo athletes exhibited a significant main effect of time for both APD (P = 0.012) and SWV (P = 0.012), regardless of side. No significant acute changes in APD or SWV were observed in the control group. For intratendinous vascularity, a significant side-by-time interaction was observed in Kendo athletes (P = 0.026): the right leg showed no significant change, whereas the left leg exhibited a progressive increase from PRE to POST (P < 0.001) and further increased at POST5 (P = 0.002). In the control group, vessel count significantly increased at POST (P = 0.023) but rapidly returned to baseline. In the three-way analyses, no significant Group × Side × Time interaction was observed for any imaging outcome.
CONCLUSION: Within Kendo athletes, morphological and mechanical responses occurred bilaterally, whereas the temporal vascular response differed between the left and right Achilles tendons. However, this side-specific vascular pattern was not shown to differ significantly from that observed in sedentary controls.

title: Hydrogels as drug carriers for cartilage repair in osteoarthritis: Applications and challenges.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent chronic degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodelling, synovial inflammation, osteophyte formation, and loss of joint function, resulting in significant pain, disability, and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Despite advances in clinical management, current therapeutic strategies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid injections, and surgical interventions, primarily provide symptomatic relief and have limited ability to prevent disease progression or regenerate damaged cartilage. In recent years, hydrogel-based drug delivery systems have emerged as promising therapeutic platforms owing to their excellent biocompatibility, biodegradability, injectability, high water content, and structural similarity to the native extracellular matrix. These properties enable hydrogels to serve as effective carriers for a wide range of therapeutic agents, including anti-inflammatory drugs, growth factors, nucleic acids, nanoparticles, exosomes, and stem cells, while providing sustained and localized drug release within the osteoarthritic joint. This review comprehensively discusses the pathophysiology of OA and highlights the major molecular signaling pathways involved in disease progression, including NF-κB, MAPK, Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, TGF-β, and JAK/STAT pathways. Furthermore, recent advances in natural, synthetic, hybrid, and stimuli-responsive hydrogels are critically examined, with particular emphasis on their applications in cartilage repair and targeted drug delivery. Emerging approaches involving nanotechnology-enabled hydrogels, gene delivery systems, stem cell-loaded constructs, and immunomodulatory biomaterials are also evaluated for their therapeutic potential and translational prospects. This review provides an integrated and up-to-date perspective on hydrogel-based strategies for cartilage regeneration and disease modification, highlighting their potential as next-generation therapeutic platforms for the long-term management of osteoarthritis.
