title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Treatment of clavicle fractures in adolescents.
abstract: Clavicle fractures constitute 10% to 15% of all fractures in adolescents. Historically, adolescent clavicle fractures have been treated non-operatively. Although recent data in the adult population has led to an increased rate of operative fixation in the adolescent population, a vast majority of these fractures in adolescents can be managed conservatively. This manuscript provides an overview of the current standard of care for clavicular fractures in adolescents in the context of sports medicine practices. To achieve this, a nonsystematic search of computerized databases of peer-reviewed articles was conducted, and a critical appraisal of existing literature was subsequently performed. Middle third clavicle fractures are by far the most common type and a vast majority of these fractures can be treated non-operatively with a sling given the robust healing and remodeling seen in adolescents. Lateral third fractures are far less common but may pose a risk for nonunion according to adult literature. Medial third fractures are the least common type and while they are typically non-displaced, patients with posteriorly displaced medial third fractures must have concomitant intrathoracic injury ruled out. Additionally, timing of the injury relative to competitive season could play a role in decision making as surgical fixation of clavicle fractures has been shown to yield faster return to play times.

title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.

title: 18-years Follow-up after Mosaicplasty in Adolescent Athletes with Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Elbow.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty is an established surgical treatment of unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions of the elbow. However, the information on the long-term outcomes is lacking. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic results after autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty in the treatment of OCD of the elbow.
METHODS: This prospective long-term follow-up study is an extension of previously published data on 10 patients treated with autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty due to advanced, unstable OCD at the capitellum from 2003-2007. Objective and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated including Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score, Quick-Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (Quick-DASH), Timmerman-Andrews Score, a Subjective Elbow Value, and Range of Motion (ROM). Radiographic signs of osteoarthritis were graded according to the Kellgren-Lawrence classification.
RESULTS: At mean 18 years (range 16.0-19.7) five patients were available for follow-up. Mean age at follow-up was 34.4, and all five patients were women. MEPS was a median 100 (range 85-100). Activities of daily life were mildly affected in two patients. Two patients had non-symptomatic osteoarthritis grade 1 and 2. Patients experienced a functioning and near-normal elbow.
CONCLUSION: The long-term results after mosaicplasty are encouraging, and we find it reasonable to recommend mosaicplasty as the surgical treatment in this group of female patients with advanced, unstable OCD lesions of the elbow. However, it is of concern that two out of five patients had non-symptomatic early radiographic signs of osteoarthritis at an early age. As this study has an inclusion rate of 50 % of the original cohort, attrition bias must be taken into consideration.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series, treatment study.
journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery

title: High-Strength Tape for Cable Structure Reconstruction During Arthroscopic Repair of L-Shaped Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract: With the innovation and progressive maturation of arthroscopic techniques, the advantages of minimally invasive surgery and accelerated rehabilitation have made arthroscopy a preferred option for patients with rotator cuff injuries. However, for complex rotator cuff tears, such as "L-shaped" tendon tears, the risk of postoperative retear remains considerable. The cable structure, serving as a "suspension bridge" within the rotator cuff, is a critical load-bearing component of the shoulder joint. This structure is frequently compromised in "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. In this report, we describe an arthroscopic technique using high-strength tape to restore the cable structure and treat "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. The key steps include using high-strength tape to reduce the retracted tendon stump and restore the cable structure, thereby re-establishing mechanical integrity, reducing tension on the repaired tendon, and minimizing the cutting effect of sutures on the tendon. Finally, the sutures from the medial-row anchor are employed to perform a "Margin Convergence" repair of the longitudinal tear component.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Relationship between lower extremity isokinetic strength ratio and dynamic balance ability in elite combat sports athletes.
abstract: Dynamic balance is essential for performance and injury prevention in combat sports, but its relationship with isokinetic strength ratios of the lower extremity and trunk is not well understood. This study investigated the associations between knee, hip, and trunk strength ratios and dynamic balance in elite combat sport athletes. Fifty-one elite judo and wushu athletes (31 males, 20 females) underwent isokinetic testing of the knee, hip, and trunk, with peak torque normalized to body mass (%body weight). Dynamic balance was assessed using the Biodex Balance System SD. Interaction effects between strength ratios and balance variables were analyzed using three-way analysis of variance. Male athletes showed greater muscle strength, whereas female athletes demonstrated better dynamic balance. Higher knee flexor-to-extensor strength ratios (≥61%) and moderate hip (35%-40%) and trunk strength ratios were associated with better dynamic balance. Significant interaction effects were found between knee and hip strength ratios. Our findings suggest that dynamic balance in elite combat sport athletes may depend on the coordinated strength balance of the knee, hip, and trunk rather than on absolute muscle strength alone.

title: From bouts to readiness to compete: temporal dynamics of stress, fatigue, recovery and monitoring-informed decisions in combat sports.
abstract: Combat-sport tournaments require decisions before responses to previous efforts have resolved. Detecting a change does not establish that an indicator predicts the next task or improves a decision. This Perspective proposes a task- and time-specific framework linking prior bouts, recovery time and subsequent demands through three evidentiary requirements. Responsiveness concerns reproducible changes beyond measurement error when an indicator represents a response to effort. Predictive validity concerns anticipation of a pre-specified subsequent outcome and added information beyond simpler measures. Decision utility concerns improved outcomes relative to usual practice. Indicators interpreted as current status or stable capacity need not respond to prior effort, but still require adequate measurement properties and prospective evaluation. Evidence from repeated bouts, recovery interventions, mental fatigue, sleep restriction and weight loss suggests that monitoring domains are not interchangeable. The framework retains discordant indicators, evaluates combinations and communicates uncertainty without global clearance labels. Three hypotheses address task and time dependence, maintained performance with increasing effort cost, and indicator-informed decisions. Medical decisions remain independent and take precedence. This is an operational extension of existing principles, not a validated predictive tool.

title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

title: Spatial transcriptomics in immune-mediated necrotising myopathy uncovers a specific necrotic signature related to immune-driven fibrosis.
abstract: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathies (IMNM) are characterised by muscle fibre necrosis, complement deposits around non-necrotic fibres, and macrophage infiltrates. Patients experience muscle damage with fibro-fatty replacement, leading to poor strength recovery, but the pathogenesis remains unclear. To investigate IMNM pathogenesis, we applied spatial transcriptomics on myositis muscle biopsies and integrated the results with published single-nucleus transcriptomic data. This combined approach enabled analysis of gene expression with spatial localisation in the muscle. Inflammatory, fibrotic, regenerative, and lipid metabolism-related signatures were identified in IMNM, distinct from other myositis, with specific distribution in necrotic and peri-necrotic regions. A unique subtype of immune-driven fibroblasts expressing SFRP4 was enriched in IMNM necrotic areas. These cells carried a strong proportion of IMNM-enriched pathological signatures, notably a complement-linked 'tumour-like' inflammatory fibroblast signature and a specific interferon response, characterised by the expression of metallothioneins. Peri-necrotic areas were characterised by pathological muscle signatures carrying interferon response and FABP4+ metabolically dysfunctional signatures. In conclusion, IMNM necrotic muscle areas are linked to a specific SFRP4-expressing fibroblast subtype interacting with macrophages, potentially driving the pathological muscle phenotype and contributing to inflammation, fibro-fatty replacement, and strength loss.

title: Statistical Parametric Mapping reveals sex-specific, phase-dependent differences in bilateral three-dimensional ground reaction force during Wushu Changbing PiJi in high-level athletes.
abstract: PiJi is a core attacking technique in Wushu Changbing competition, but continuous waveform evidence remains limited regarding the sex-specific phase characteristics of bilateral 3D ground reaction force (GRF) during PiJi performed with maximal voluntary effort (MVE). This study aimed to compare continuous changes in trailing-foot, lead-foot, and net bilateral GRF between high-level male and female athletes during PiJi performed with MVE. In this cross-sectional, laboratory-based observational study, 44 right-hand-dominant athletes, including 22 male athletes and 22 female athletes, performed PiJi with MVE, yielding 616 valid trials. Bilateral 3D GRF was recorded using two force plates. Each trial was time-normalized and linearly interpolated to 143 equally spaced nodes, and within-participant mean waveforms were calculated before between-group differences were analyzed using statistical parametric mapping. Primary analyses used random-field-theory inference, with sensitivity examined using 5,000 permutation tests. After Bonferroni correction, phase-specific sex differences were detected in trailing-foot, lead-foot, and net bilateral 3D GRF. Scalar localization showed that male athletes had higher trailing-foot Fy during the middle phase (33.98%-47.04%) and higher trailing-foot Fx (62.41%-71.99%) and net bilateral Fx (54.18%-70.41%) during the middle-to-late phase; female athletes showed only a brief period of higher trailing-foot vertical Fz during the middle phase (42.11%-44.61%). Although lead-foot 3D GRF differed overall, no confirmatory difference was localized to any single scalar component. These findings indicate that sex-related GRF differences in high-level PiJi were concentrated mainly in specific horizontal-plane phases of trailing-foot and net bilateral force, whereas the lead-foot difference was identified only at the overall 3D GRF level. These results provide kinetic evidence for phase-specific assessment of PiJi technique and suggest that training monitoring and mechanistic research should consider foot, direction, and movement phase rather than relying only on peak force or discrete variables. Future studies integrating multimodal measures and sport-specific performance may further clarify the functional significance of bilateral force-generation patterns.

title: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders among civil servants attending healthcare facilities in Bangladesh: An observational cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a major occupational health concern worldwide, significantly affecting employees' well-being and productivity. Government employees in Bangladesh are particularly vulnerable to WMSDs due to the sedentary or repetitive nature of their work (e.g., prolonged computer use, repetitive typing, and manual mechanical tasks).ObjectiveThis study aimed to determine the clinical distribution, patterns, and associated factors of WMSDs among government employees in Bangladesh and evaluate the subjective impact on workers' productivity and quality of life.MethodsA retrospective descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted at the Government Employees Hospital in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Participants were recruited using consecutive sampling from government employees attending the Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation Department. Descriptive and inferential statistics (Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests via R software) were used to examine the distribution of conditions like low back pain, knee osteoarthritis, cervical spondylosis, frozen shoulder. Productivity and quality of life were assessed through structured clinical interviews, while demographic characteristics, work type, and employment grade were analyzed to identify associated factors.ResultsNonspecific low back pain was the most prevalent condition (27.23%), particularly among retired employees (34.62%) and sedentary workers (26.97%). Knee osteoarthritis (10.81%) and cervical spondylosis (8.97%) were more common among older and dynamic workers. The most commonly affected sites were the lower back (43.73%), knees, shoulders, and neck. Disease patterns varied significantly by age, and government service grade.ConclusionThe high proportion of diagnosed cases among Bangladeshi government employees underscores the need for interventions including ergonomic modifications, regular health assessments, and early screening strategies to reduce WMSD impact and inform public sector health policies.

title: Sleep Management in Paralympic Sports: Knowledge, Monitoring Practices, and Perceived Barriers among Coaches and Healthcare Staff.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Coaches and healthcare staff play a crucial role in disseminating knowledge about the importance of sleep to develop a precise balance between recovery and the demands imposed by sports training.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the knowledge on sleep, jet lag, and sleep hygiene (SH) among coaches and healthcare staff in Paralympic sports; 2) to identify whether the sleep of Paralympic athletes is monitored, and which instruments are commonly used; and 3) to identify the main barriers faced in sleep management.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The present cross-sectional study was conducted with 60 coaches and healthcare staff who work in the preparation of elite Paralympic athletes. The participants filled out the Sleep Beliefs Scale and a structured questionnaire before traveling to the 2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games.
RESULTS: Coaches and healthcare staff understand the importance of sleep for sports performance and recovery, but only 56% monitored their sleep. The most commonly used methods were subjective. Lack of adherence and commitment among Paralympic athletes (27%) and lack of training (19%) were the main barriers to sleep management.
CONCLUSION: Coaches and healthcare staff are aware of the importance of sleep; however, educational programs are needed to improve the training of coaching and healthcare staff for efficient sleep management and to raise awareness among Paralympic athletes about the importance of sleep.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: When Proxies Overshadow Actual Performance: Reaffirming First Principles in Applied Sport Science.
abstract:
PURPOSE: In recent years, sport science has witnessed a growing emphasis on derived mechanical metrics and complex analytical approaches, often accompanied by claims that direct performance measures, such as jump height or sprint time are misleading or less informative than the proxies intended to explain them. This trend has contributed to a progressive shift away from the primary outcomes of athletic testing and toward secondary descriptors, frequently interpreted as superior indicators of performance. Using the vertical jump as a representative example, this commentary revisits fundamental foundations of classical mechanics and applied sport science to clarify the distinction between performance outcomes and mechanistic descriptors. The purpose of this commentary is to reinforce a fundamental principle of performance assessment: when the intended construct is task performance, direct outcomes, such as vertical jump height, horizontal jump distance, and sprint time should remain the primary reference. Mechanistic measures should be selected when they provide reliable and actionable information about how that outcome was achieved or why it changed.
CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: Actual performance outcomes, such as jump height, jump distance, and sprint time are the most meaningful, interpretable, and relevant indicators of athletic performance. Mechanistic variables and detailed analytical approaches may provide valuable insights into underlying movement strategies and efficiency, but they should complement, rather than replace, direct performance measures. Following Occam's razor, applied sport science should continue to embrace scientific advances while avoiding the unnecessary promotion of complex, time-consuming, and expensive technologies as indispensable tools for coaches and practitioners, thereby preserving confidence in simple, valid, and accessible measures of athletic performance.

title: Aerobic exercise preconditioning enhances skeletal muscle resistance and recovery after contusion: involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Compared with passive recovery after injury, exercise preconditioning may provide an active strategy for improving the subsequent response of skeletal muscle to injury. This study aimed to investigate the effects of aerobic exercise preconditioning (AEP) on skeletal muscle injury (SMI) and post-injury repair, with particular focus on the involvement of the SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and changes in PGC-1α acetylation.
METHODS: This study initially investigated the effects of continuous aerobic exercise on skeletal muscle in healthy mice. Subsequently, the influence of AEP on injury severity and regenerative repair of the gastrocnemius muscle was examined in mice with SMI. Western blotting was used to determine the expression levels of SIRT1 and PGC-1α proteins, immunoprecipitation was performed to assess the acetylation status of PGC-1α, and qRT-PCR was used to analyze the expression of genes associated with mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers and muscle regeneration. Finally, the involvement of SIRT1 signaling in the AEP-associated response to SMI was further examined using the pharmacological SIRT1 inhibitor EX527.
RESULTS: Continuous aerobic exercise was associated with increased SIRT1/PGC-1α signaling and changes in mitochondrial biogenesis-related markers in the gastrocnemius muscle of healthy mice. AEP was associated with reduced injury-related changes and an improved post-injury repair profile in mice with SMI. During the early stage after injury, AEP was accompanied by sustained SIRT1/ PGC-1α signaling and reduced PGC-1α acetylation. Pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 with EX527 partially attenuated the AEP-associated protective and reparative effects on the injured gastrocnemius muscle.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that AEP establishes an adaptive state in skeletal muscle that is associated with reduced injury-related damage and an enhanced post-injury reparative response. The SIRT1/PGC-1α axis and altered PGC-1α acetylation may contribute to these AEP-associated effects.

title: Beyond Movement Behaviours: Unravelling the Prospective Links Between 24-Hour Behavioural Composition and Affective Dynamics in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: While the full spectrum of 24-hour movement behaviours - encompassing sleep (SLP), sedentary behaviour (SB), light physical activity (LPA), structured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (S-MVPA), and unstructured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (US-MVPA) - is consistently linked to daily affective states in adolescent athletes, existing literature has rarely examined these behaviours as an interdependent time-use composition, and largely fails to disentangle the distinct effects of structured versus unstructured MVPA subdomains on emotional outcomes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Using a repeated-measures prospective daily design, this study included 161 adolescent athletes (101 males and 60 females). Accelerometers were used to quantify 24-h movement behaviours. Four affective dimensions were assessed through ecological momentary assessment (EMA): high-arousal positive affect, low-arousal positive affect, high-arousal negative affect, and low-arousal negative affect. Bayesian multilevel compositional models were used to estimate between- and within-person associations, while isotemporal substitution analyses evaluated the estimated effects of reallocating time between behaviours on next-day affect.
RESULTS: Associations between 24-h behaviour compositions and next-day affect were more evident at the within-person level. A higher relative proportion of LPA was associated with higher high-arousal positive affect (0.305, 95% Bayesian credible interval [CrI] 0.255 to 0.354) and low-arousal positive affect (0.292, 95% CrI 0.245 to 0.338), and lower high-arousal negative affect (-0.231, 95% CrI -0.260 to -0.203) and low-arousal negative affect (-0.210, 95% CrI -0.236 to -0.185). In 30-min substitution analyses, reallocating time from other behaviours to LPA generally showed more favourable associations with next-day affect at both between- and within-person levels, although the associations varied across substitution pairs and affective dimensions. These findings highlight LPA as the behaviour most consistently associated with favourable next-day affect.
CONCLUSIONS: Daily 24-h movement behaviour composition was prospectively associated with next-day affect in adolescent athletes. LPA showed the most consistent favourable associations with next-day affect, particularly when replacing SB. Promoting LPA may represent a feasible strategy for supporting affective wellbeing without adding to existing training demands.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Creating Consensus: Establishing a Definition of Sports Pharmacy and Its Emerging Role in Sports Medicine.
abstract: Sports pharmacy has become an increasingly recognized specialty within the broader pharmacy profession and serves as a complementary discipline to sport medicine. Yet, the field has lacked a formally established, internationally accepted definition. The absence of standardized terminology has hindered academic integration, interprofessional collaboration, and policy development. This work aimed to establish the first consensus-derived definition of sports pharmacy, accompanied by a responsibility statement to guide future education, certification, and research. In 2024, the US Sports Pharmacy Group (USSPG), comprising pharmacists, academics, anti-doping professionals, student pharmacists, and competitive athletes from diverse US states and international settings, convened a discrete subgroup, the Define Sports Pharmacy Taskforce, to lead the development of a formal definition of sports pharmacy. The taskforce conducted a thematic analysis of existing literature and reviewed 123 open-ended member responses collected between 2022 and 2024. Eight recurring practice themes emerged and informed iterative drafting cycles. Draft definitions were subsequently reviewed by interprofessional stakeholders, including physicians, elite athletes, and anti-doping practitioners. The resulting definition emphasizes medication management, anti-doping advocacy, interprofessional collaboration, athlete-centered ethical care, and the use of therapeutic and pharmacological strategies to optimize performance, support recovery, and protect sports integrity across all levels of physical activity. This consensus-derived framework provides standardized terminology to support the development of educational pathways, establish certification standards, and promote the integration of pharmacists into athlete support teams.

title: Delayed Diagnosis of Achilles Tendon Rupture in a 75-Year-Old Patient with Bimalleolar Ankle Fracture: A Case Report.
abstract:
CASE: A 75-year-old woman sustained a minimally displaced bimalleolar ankle fracture after a fall. An ipsilateral Achilles tendon rupture was missed until day 26, when persistent heel pain and inability to plantarflex prompted an MRI, revealing a rupture with a 5.5-cm gap. Both injuries were treated nonoperatively using controlled ankle motion (CAM) boots, heel wedges, progressive weight bearing, and rehabilitation. At 12 months, the patient had resumed independent ambulation.
CONCLUSION: All ankle fracture patients should undergo systematic Achilles tendon assessment with early follow-up reassessment and a low threshold for advanced imaging when the initial examination is limited.

title: Flexible and stretchable bioelectronics for sports wearable monitoring: Materials, Device Engineering, and Intelligent Wearable Platforms.
abstract: Modern sports science is undergoing a paradigm shift from subjective coaching to objective, data-driven precision training. Consequently, wearable electronics for acquiring precise data during sports activities are attracting attention. However, conventional rigid wearables inherently suffer from mechanical mismatches between rigid wearables and the soft, deformable human skin, inducing severe motion artifacts and restricting natural biomechanics during high-intensity athletic activities. To address these limitations from a comprehensive perspective, this review systematically summarizes and analyzes recent advancements in next-generation flexible and stretchable bioelectronics tailored specifically for sports applications. We systematically examine the substrate materials, structural engineering designs, and device-level optimization strategies required to withstand repetitive strain, shear, and sweat-intensive environments. Building upon these conformable bio-interfaces, we discuss three core sensing modalities: electrochemical sensors for real-time analysis of sweat biomarkers, biophysical sensors for continuous electrophysiological and hemodynamic monitoring, and electromechanical sensors for high-fidelity kinematic and impact tracking. Furthermore, we discuss body-derived energy harvesting strategies to power sports wearables and wireless communication systems for continuous athletic monitoring. The importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning is increasing, as these techniques enable the removal of motion artifacts and facilitate objective analysis of athletic data for training and health monitoring applications. By evaluating targeted applications across aerobic and anaerobic exercise, cognitive state assessment, and post-exercise recovery, this review demonstrates how next-generation sports wearables contribute to the shift in sports science from reactive treatment toward proactive, data-driven performance enhancement and injury prevention.

title: Pre-season friendly match-play as a double-edged sword: Performance gains and inflammatory cost in semi-professional soccer players (a natural experiment).
abstract: Pre-season training prepares soccer players for competition, but the longitudinal effects of friendly match exposure remain unclear. We investigated whether cumulative late pre-season match-play is associated with physiological adaptation in semi-professional players. Twenty-four male players from a randomly selected semi-professional team competing at national level were assessed at pre-season start, mid-pre-season and pre-competition. Measurements included body composition, physical performance, aerobic fitness and blood markers reflecting muscle damage, inflammation, hormonal status and haematological adaptation. Based on cumulative playing time across eight friendly matches, as determined by coaching staff, players were classified retrospectively into extended play (EP) or limited play (LP) groups. Controlling for mid-pre-season baseline, the EP group showed significantly lower pre-competition values for body mass ( η p 2 = 0.276), body fat ( η p 2 = 0.294) and 35 m sprint time ( η p 2 = 0.129) and higher values for lower-limb power (dominant/non-dominant; η p 2 = 0.219-0.424), velocity at maximal oxygen uptake ( η p 2 = 0.441) and at second ventilatory threshold ( η p 2 = 0.708), serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase ( η p 2 = 0.296), myoglobin ( η p 2 = 0.199), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein ( η p 2 = 0.920), interleukin-6 ( η p 2 = 0.893), tumour necrosis factor-α ( η p 2 = 0.937) and red blood cell count ( η p 2 = 0.190) (all P ≤ 0.038). Across all participants, total match-play time was correlated significantly with reductions in body fat (r = -0.47) and increases in lower-limb power (r = 0.44-0.67), second ventilatory threshold (r = 0.55) and inflammatory markers (r = 0.79-0.86) (all P ≤ 0.033). Greater friendly match-play exposure during pre-season was associated with favourable physiological adaptations and a more pronounced physiological and inflammatory response. These findings support friendly match-play as a meaningful physiological stimulus and highlight the importance of balancing match exposure with recovery during pre-season preparation.

title: A Six-Day High-Intensity Interval Training Microcycle Improves Selected Indicators of Endurance Performance in Well-Trained Female Cross-Country Skiers and Biathletes.
abstract: We compared the effects of a 6-day high-intensity interval training (HIT) microcycle followed by a 5-day active recovery period (HITblock) with a time-matched period of continued regular training (REG) on endurance performance in well-trained female cross-country skiers and biathletes. Seventeen athletes (maximal oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 max ): 55.1 (5.2) mL·min-1 kg-1) were assigned to either HITblock or REG. No differences in training volume or intensity were observed between the groups during the 4 weeks preceding the intervention. During the intervention, HITblock completed five HIT sessions over 6 days (6 × 5-min work intervals; target rate of perceived exertion:17-18), with increased HIT replacing part of their habitual training and thereby reducing overall training load, whereas REG continued habitual training, including 3-4 moderate- or high-intensity interval sessions. Endurance performance was assessed during roller ski skating and included 15-min time-trial average velocity (velocity15-min), velocity at 4 mmol·L-1 blood lactate (velocity4mmol), and velocity during the final minute of incremental V ˙ O 2 max testing ( velocity V ˙ O 2 max ). HITblock demonstrated greater improvements than REG in velocity V ˙ O 2 max (3.6 (2.1)% versus 1.2 (1.6)%, p = 0.024) and velocity4mmol (4.4 (2.9)% versus 0.0 (4.4)%, p = 0.023), whereas changes in velocity15-min did not differ between groups (5.4 (5.0)% versus 1.3 (3.4)%, p = 0.083). An exploratory composite performance index combining these outcomes demonstrated superior improvements in HITblock compared with REG (4.5 (2.8)% versus 0.9 (2.6)%, p = 0.017). These findings indicate that a 6-day HIT microcycle followed by a 5-day active recovery period is associated with greater improvements in selected endurance performance indicators compared with continued regular training in well-trained female cross-country skiers and biathletes.

title: Gender Differences in Sports Injuries of the Foot and Ankle.
abstract: This article examines sex-based differences in foot and ankle injuries among female athletes, emphasizing the role of anatomic, hormonal, biomechanical, and sociocultural factors. Female athletes are disproportionately affected by ankle sprains, chronic instability, and bone stress injuries. Conditions such as relative energy deficiency in sport and the female athlete triad contribute to injury risk and long-term health consequences but remain under-recognized. This article highlights disparities in research, treatment, and outcomes, calling for improved screening, sex-specific prevention strategies, and greater inclusion of female subjects in sports medicine research to inform evidence-based care and optimize outcomes for female athletes.

title: Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery: Are Marathon and Trail Running Different?
abstract: Although trail and road are two running disciplines, they have distinct characteristics potentially leading to different physiological impacts that have never been examined. The aim of the present study was to compare neuromuscular fatigue and recovery between a marathon and two trail runs of equivalent effort (29 km; ± 1,400 m). Forty-one trained runners, specialized in either road or trail running, performed a simulated treadmill marathon (MARASIM), a simulated treadmill trail run (TRAILSIM), or a trail run in natural conditions (TRAILNAT), depending on their speciality. Neuromuscular fatigue, i.e. changes in maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), voluntary activation (VA) and peak twitch (Tw) of the knee extensors (KE) and plantar flexors (PF), blood markers of muscle damage, jump performance, and force-velocity profile (FVP) were assessed before (PRE), immediately after (POST), one (+1 day), two (+2 days), and seven days (+7 days) following the runs. Muscle pain questionnaires were administered at PRE and during the month following the run. MARASIM showed significantly greater decreases in KE VA (-23.5% vs. -9.2% vs. -13.0%) and jump height (-11.7%; +11.4%; +5.9%, for squat jump), and significantly higher increases in blood markers of muscle damage (+1,726 UI.L -1; +641 UI.L -1; +363 UI.L -1; at +1 day) compared to TRAILSIM and TRAILNAT, respectively. The return to baseline occurred later in MARASIM for KE VA and jump height. Muscle soreness values also returned to baseline earlier in TRAILNAT and TRAILSIM compared to MARASIM. No differences between groups existed in KE Pt and MVC, in any PF neuromuscular fatigue variables, and FVP. Overall, marathon running appears to induce greater acute neuromuscular alterations than trail running, mostly on KE, with a slower return to baseline values.

title: The Sleep and Diet of Elite Female Australian Rules Football Athletes Differ With Age and Season Phase.
abstract: The Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) competition is comprised of a short, intensive competitive season, highlighting the importance of proper fuelling and recovery to support performance. Little is known about the dietary and sleep habits of AFLW athletes across a season, and the influence that age has on these behaviours. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the effects of season phase and age on dietary intake and sleep in elite AFLW athletes. Dietary intake and sleep were assessed in 22 AFLW athletes (25.9 ± 5.0 y) over 10 nights, including five consecutive nights during both pre-season and in-season. Dietary intake was quantified through self-reported food diaries using a smartphone application (Easy Diet Diary), and sleep via a wearable monitoring device (Oura ring). Restricted maximum likelihood mixed models were used to determine variations in dietary intake and sleep in AFLW players between season phases (i.e., pre-season vs. in-season) and age. In-season protein (115.15 ± 35.14 vs. 126.48 ± 40.10 g, p = 0.026) and fat intakes (72.93 ± 29.55 vs. 83.43 ± 33.14 g, p = 0.012) were significantly lower compared to pre-season, with no differences in sleep measures observed between season phases. While age did not influence dietary intake, each additional year of age was associated with 8 min less sleep (p = 0.001) and 4 min earlier wake times (p = 0.032). These findings suggest that protein and fat intakes fluctuate across the seasons, with increasing age being a non-modifiable risk factor for shorter sleep durations within AFLW athletes.

title: Osteoarthritis-Microenvironment-Triggered Phase Alteration of Injectable Conductive Hydrogel for Attenuating Cartilage Degradation.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is associated with excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which contributes substantially to chondrocyte dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cartilage degradation. Although stimuli-responsive hydrogels have emerged as promising platforms for OA therapy, conventional hydrogel-based systems exhibit limited sensitivity and require external detection equipment, highlighting the need for a simple, sensitive, and directly observable monitoring system. To address these challenges, we developed a ROS-triggered, in situ-forming gel-sol transition of a polydopamine (PDA)-loaded, diselenide-crosslinked polymer dot (PD) injectable hydrogel (HGC-PDA@PD or OA gel) as a monitorable theranostic for OA therapy at physiological temperature (37°C). The monitorable OA microenvironment-responsive hydrogel relied on interactions between the high ROS levels in OA cartilage and the OA gel, which triggered diselenide bond cleavage and the release of PDA from PD, causing a unique gel-sol transition of the OA gel. Owing to PDA release after diselenide breakage, the fluorescence and electroconductivity of the OA gel changed, which could serve as additional signals during OA detection. In vitro studies demonstrated the sensitive gel-sol transition of OA gel towards OA-induced immature articular chondrocytes (IL-1β/siSOD1/siCatalase-transfected iMACs). Furthermore, the OA gel showed a distinct gel-sol transition in cartilage of an in vivo OA mouse model compared with that in control mice. The lower transcription levels of cartilage matrix-degrading enzymes (ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, MMP-3, and MMP-13) observed after OA gel injection confirmed that the OA gel could scavenge ROS and attenuate cartilage damage, revealing its potential application for dual-function OA diagnosis and rehabilitation.

title: Ethanol-induced alterations in mesenchymal stromal cells and the effects of aspalathin: implications for alcohol-associated osteonecrosis.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Alcohol-associated osteonecrosis is a debilitating condition characterized by progressive bone destruction. Although mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) play a critical role in tissue repair, the effects of chronic alcohol exposure on MSCs and their responsiveness to microenvironmental signals remain unclear.
METHODS: MSCs were exposed to ethanol (EtOH) to evaluate changes in viable cell number, ROS-related fluorescence signals, and the expression of mitochondrial-related, senescence-associated, and chemokine signaling-related molecules. CXCL12 expression was examined in human femoral head specimens and ethanol-exposed osteocyte-like cells. The effects of aspalathin (ASP) on EtOH-induced alterations in MSCs were also investigated.
RESULTS: EtOH exposure reduced viable MSC number and increased ROS-related fluorescence signals. It was also associated with decreased expression of ATP5A and CXCR4 and increased expression of p16. CXCL12 expression was higher in alcohol-associated osteonecrosis tissue than in osteoarthritis tissue and appeared qualitatively increased in ethanol-exposed osteocyte-like cells. These findings indicate altered CXCL12 and CXCR4 expression across the tissue and in vitro experimental settings. ASP treatment attenuated the EtOH-induced reduction in the CCK-8 signal, was associated with attenuation of ROS-related fluorescence signals, significantly restored ATP5A expression, suppressed p16 expression, and showed a non-significant trend toward recovery of CXCR4 expression.
CONCLUSIONS: Ethanol exposure was associated with alterations in the cellular state of MSCs, accompanied by changes in ROS-related fluorescence signals and the expression of mitochondrial-related, senescence-associated, and chemokine signaling-related molecules. ASP partially attenuated some of these ethanol-induced alterations. Further studies are required to clarify the functional significance of these findings and to validate them in vivo.

title: Exercise-related signal abnormality (ERSA)-associated acute thigh muscle injuries in a subset of professional soccer players.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Exercise-related signal abnormality (ERSA) is a relatively new MRI entity described in professional soccer players. We report a subset of players who sustained acute muscle injuries and ERSA lesions in the same muscle.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted from July 2024 to July 2026 to identify all MRI studies of professional soccer players with an acute thigh muscle injury and ERSA lesion in the same muscle. Anatomical site, laterality, ERSA lesion subtype and length, and acute muscle injury grade as per the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) were recorded.
RESULTS: There were 18 ERSA-associated acute thigh muscle injuries in 16 soccer players (12 males, 4 females; median age 20.5 years). Affected muscles were the rectus femoris (n = 12), adductor longus (n = 5), and semitendinosus (n = 1). Type C ERSA lesions (n = 13) and BAMIC grade 2b (n = 8) muscle injuries were the most common. All acute muscle injuries were located within the ERSA lesions. No intratendinous extension was observed. Median ERSA lesion length was 21.5 cm and median acute muscle injury length was 7.0 cm. The main ERSA-associated muscle injury patterns were pre-degloving (n = 6) and myofascial (n = 6) injuries of the rectus femoris and distal myotendinous junction injuries of the adductor longus (n = 4).
CONCLUSION: We describe a new muscle injury pattern, termed ERSA-associated acute thigh muscle injuries, in a cohort of professional soccer players. Distinct injury patterns were observed in the rectus femoris and adductor longus.

title: Limb ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats is partially mediated by enhancing necroptosis via phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL.
abstract: Limb ischemia-reperfusion injury (L-IRI) causes severe skeletal muscle damage and functional impairment through activation of regulated cell-death and inflammatory pathways. Necroptosis is a regulated form of necrotic cell death mediated through the receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-RIPK3-mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) signaling axis. Prior experimental studies have shown that Necrostatin-1 (Nec-1) attenuates acute skeletal muscle ischemia-reperfusion injury in rats. However, how Nec-1-sensitive protection relates to RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, circulating muscle injury markers, inflammatory responses, histological damage, and functional recovery during the early postischemic period remains incompletely defined. In this study, we used a rat model of unilateral hindlimb ischemia involving 3 h of ischemia followed by reperfusion for up to 7 days to evaluate these interrelated responses. Nec-1 was administered before ischemia and after reperfusion. L-IRI resulted in elevated plasma creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase levels, severe histopathological injury, increased TUNEL staining, impaired grip strength, and reduced Modified Tarlov scores. These changes were accompanied by increased phosphorylation of RIPK1 and MLKL, activation of inflammatory signaling pathways, and altered expression of injury-associated inflammatory mediators. Nec-1 treatment reduced RIPK1/MLKL-associated signaling, inflammatory mediator expression, circulating muscle injury markers, and histological injury while preserving muscle architecture and improving functional recovery. These findings support and extend previous evidence that Nec-1-sensitive necroptosis-associated signaling contributes to early skeletal muscle injury following L-IRI. Pharmacologic targeting of regulated necrotic and inflammatory pathways warrants further investigation as a potential adjunct strategy for limiting acute skeletal muscle injury after limb reperfusion.NEW & NOTEWORTHY This study links Necrostatin-1 (Nec-1)-sensitive receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)/mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL)-associated signaling with biochemical, histological, inflammatory, and functional outcomes after rat hindlimb ischemia-reperfusion injury. Nec-1 reduced RIPK1 and MLKL phosphorylation, muscle injury, and early functional impairment. These findings extend prior skeletal-muscle studies by integrating molecular pathway activation with longitudinal functional recovery while supporting a contribution of RIPK1-associated necroptotic signaling.

title: Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy for Rapid Screening of S1-Class Anabolic Agents.
abstract: The abuse of S1-class anabolic agents poses significant health threats to athletes and is strictly prohibited by World Anti-Doping Organization (WADA). In this study, we developed a surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) method based on silver coated gold nanostars (GNS@Ag) core-shell nanoparticles for the rapid screening of four representative S1 agents: danazol, fluoxymesterone, zilpaterol, and androsterone. The synthesized nanomaterials feature sharp plasmonic hotspots that afford substantial SERS signal enhancement, enabling detection limits as low as~10-5 to ~10-7 g/mL. Owing to the fingerprint specificity of Raman spectroscopy, the method distinguishes different analytes and their mixtures by characteristic peak patterns. Coupled with principal component analysis (PCA), the approach enables robust discrimination of anabolic agents. Successful application to spiked milk samples demonstrates good recovery, rapid response, and practical utility, highlighting the potential of this SERS strategy as a promising tool for on-site anti-doping screening.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy

title: Longitudinal association between vertical jump performance and sprint acceleration performance in sprinters.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed at investigating the associations between changes in sprint performance and changes in vertical jump performances and to clarify whether the vertical jump performances would reflect better sprint acceleration performance.
METHODS: To examine the association between changes in sprint performance and vertical jump performance, two experimental sessions per participant were conducted using an identical protocol with a one- or two-month interval. Seventeen male sprinters performed a 60-m sprint and 3 vertical jump tests in each test session.
RESULTS: The change in 60-m sprint time was correlated with changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) height (r=-0.573) and ankle continuous rebound jump (AJ) contact time (r=0.660). Changes in sprint acceleration were correlated with changes in squat jump (SJ) height from the 10th to 16th steps (r=0.495-0.676), with changes in CMJ height from the 13th to 16th steps (r=0.509-0.587), with changes in AJ height from the 15th to 19th steps (r=0.493-0.583), with changes in AJ contact time from the 8th to 14th steps (r=-0.499 to -0.570), and with changes in AJ index from the 15th to 19th steps (r=0.496-0.627).
CONCLUSIONS: The SJ and CMJ heights, as well as AJ contact time, may likely be indicators of better sprint acceleration performance during the middle acceleration section, while AJ height and index are likely useful for indirectly assessing sprint acceleration performance during the final acceleration section. Sprinters and coaches can use these vertical jumps for monitoring changes in sprint performance for the entire distance and specific acceleration sections.

title: Stem cell therapy attenuates cerebellar histological alterations and blood-brain barrier disruption in experimental fibromyalgia: involvement of mast cells, autophagy, and NLRP3/IL-1β neuroinflammatory pathway.
abstract: Fibromyalgia is a prevalent and debilitating condition that results in generalized musculoskeletal pain, trouble sleeping, exhaustion, psychological challenges, and social problems. As a consequence of fibromyalgia's substantial therapeutic and socioeconomic burden caused by its high prevalence, uncertain etiology, wide spectrum of clinical manifestations, and sophisticated therapy, a considerable interest has emerged in investigating novel aspects of its pathophysiology, particularly those related to anxiety, depression, and cerebellar histological alterations. Such investigations may contribute to the development of effective therapeutic strategies, including the use of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) as a promising treatment approach. Rats were randomly divided into three groups: control, fibromyalgia and fibromyalgia-stem cell groups. Behavioral assessment was carried out. Cerebellar cortices were collected for histological, immunohistochemical, and morphometric analysis. Fibromyalgia group revealed anxiety-like behavioral changes, and neurodegenerative changes with blood-brain barrier (BBB) affection. Furthermore, NLRP3 and IL-1β immune-expression were significantly increased, with significant increase in the total number of mast cells with marked degranulation. Additionally, there was a significant decrease in Calbindin D-28k (CB), Beclin-1 and LC3 immune-expression. Fibromyalgia-stem cells group revealed amelioration in behavioral alterations, histological improvement, significant decrease in CD117, NLRP3 and IL-1β immune-expression, besides a significant increase in CB, Beclin-1 and LC3 immune-expression. This study represents one of the first experimental studies investigating the potential therapeutic value of BMSCs therapy in fibromyalgia-related cerebellar damage through neuroprotective mechanisms involving enhancement of autophagy, mast cell deactivation, and suppression of NLRP3/IL-1β mediated neuroinflammation with improvement of BBB structural integrity.

title: Speed at the edge of stability: a recovery-limited model of metabolic flux in the cheetah.
abstract: The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) achieves unmatched terrestrial speed through anatomical and muscular specialization for explosive power. Its type IIX glycolytic muscle phenotype, phosphocreatine (PCr) buffering and rapid glycolysis supply adenosine triphosphate at exceptionally high rates. This design enables acceleration but carries a metabolic cost: PCr is depleted, inorganic phosphate (Pi) and proton balance are disturbed, lactate is redistributed, and glucose and glycogen are used. We propose that feeding ecology may add to this cost. After a successful hunt, a substantial carcass meal imposes a second load through gastric acid secretion, the alkaline tide, pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate flux, bile acid signalling, and amino acid and lipid processing. Recovery starts when the chase ends, but its components resolve at different rates. PCr resynthesis and lactate transport may begin within minutes, whereas acid-base and electrolyte normalization, glycogen replenishment and intermediary-metabolite clearance may take longer. Feeding may therefore begin while slower recovery processes remain active, allowing the two loads to overlap. The model predicts that shorter hunt-to-feed or inter-meal intervals will increase the magnitude, duration or cumulative carry-over of acid-base, electrolyte and metabolomic perturbations. Direct cheetah evidence includes the fast-glycolytic muscle phenotype, high spot urinary creatinine concentrations, abundant urinary organic acids and altered acylcarnitine profiles. The timing and interaction of sprint recovery, digestion and metabolite clearance remain unmeasured. This Perspective integrates the adaptations that permit exceptional speed with their potential metabolic costs and provides a testable framework for evaluating how feeding ecology and managed feeding schedules influence recovery.

title: Periostin regulation by CEBPB and RACK1 and the effects of periostin-rich exosomes in osteoarthritis models.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Osteoarthritis (OA) involves chondrocyte stress and disrupted intercellular communication, but the proteins associated with synovial fluid-derived exosomes remain incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVES: We investigated periostin regulation in chondrocyte models and cellular responses relevant to OA following exposure to periostin-rich exosomes.
METHODS: Exosomes isolated from synovial fluid samples from 15 patients with OA and 5 healthy volunteers (K-L grade 0) were analyzed using label-free proteomics. Human cartilage single-cell transcriptomic data, chondrocyte stress and serial-passage models, promoter-reporter assays, co-immunoprecipitation, protein-turnover assays, RNA sequencing, pathway-inhibition experiments, and destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) studies were used for follow-up.
RESULTS: Exploratory proteomics identified periostin as a candidate protein, whose abundance was also elevated in models associated with chondrocyte senescence. CEBPB increased periostin expression and POSTN promoter-reporter activity. RACK1 co-precipitated with periostin; RACK1 overexpression slowed periostin degradation and reduced its ubiquitination. Periostin-rich exosomes increased chondrocyte catabolic activity and senescence-associated changes, increased macrophage inflammatory markers, and increased endothelial cell migration and tube formation in vitro. In DMM mice, intra-articular delivery of short hairpin RNA (shRNA) constructs targeting Cebpb or Rack1 reduced cartilage damage, whereas periostin-rich exosome supplementation partially attenuated these effects. Representative joint-tissue immunoblots showed lower CEBPB or RACK1 expression in the corresponding shRNA groups and higher periostin abundance following exosome supplementation. A p38 inhibitor or a MEK/ERK inhibitor partially attenuated chondrocyte responses to exosome treatment.
CONCLUSION: CEBPB promotes periostin expression, whereas RACK1 increases periostin protein stability and contributes to p38/ERK-associated responses to periostin-rich exosomes in chondrocyte models. Intra-articular targeting of Cebpb or Rack1 reduced cartilage damage in DMM mice.

title: Metabolic Bone Health in Female Patients: Focus on Foot and Ankle.
abstract: Metabolic bone health is crucial for the overall well-being of female patients. Female athletes and young females are of particular interest, as their skeletal systems are still developing and are sensitive to the hormonal and physical stress of training and diet. Stress fractures occur with higher frequency in females with risk factors such as low bone mineral density (BMD). When low bone mineral density occurs along with menstrual irregularities and relative energy deficiency, it completes the female triad (23, 27, and 28). Any discussion of female BMD and metabolic bone health must include the female triad.

title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis.
abstract: Skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity that relies on adult stem cells known as satellite cells (SCs), which differentiate into myogenic progenitors to drive muscle repair. How varying energy availability alters myogenesis, however, remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that intermittent fasting (IF) in mice upregulates a myogenic gene program, including Myomixer, a muscle-specific fusogen that facilitates the merging of progenitor cells into myofibers. IF enhances the regeneration of injured muscles by expanding the SC population and promoting the proliferation and fusion of myogenic progenitors. These effects are absent in an SC-depletion model. We show that fasting-induced EDA2R-NIK signaling increases Myomixer expression and fusion in myoblasts. Notably, mice lacking EDA2R or NIK fail to respond to the myogenic effects of IF. Furthermore, our data suggest that mice with Duchenne muscular dystrophy also benefit from an IF regimen. Therefore, IF-induced regeneration holds potential for aiding recovery from muscle damage.

title: Age-Dependent Alterations in Glutathione Metabolites Following Muscle Injury.
abstract: Age-related impairments in antioxidant defences contribute to delayed tissue repair and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress following muscle injury. Glutathione (GSH), a key cellular antioxidant, plays a central role in redox homeostasis and recovery processes. GSH is synthesized through a sequential process involving glutamic acid and cysteine, catalyzed by the rate-limiting enzyme glutamate cysteine ligase (GCL) to form γ-glutamyl cysteine (γGC), which subsequently combines with glycine to produce GSH. Using metabolomic profiling and acute skeletal muscle injury in mice, this study characterized age-dependent alterations in GSH biosynthesis. Clustering analysis identified that muscle from 12-month-old mice have a delayed GSH synthesis profile in response to injury compared to 3-month-old mice, with an age-dependent delay in γGC accumulation. This suggests that aging negatively influences metabolite profiles within the GSH synthesis pathway. As γGC lies downstream of this enzymatic step, its supplementation may bypass the GCL bottleneck. To test this, C2C12 myoblasts were treated with γGC (from 1-100 µg/mL), however this did not affect myoblast proliferation or differentiation. These data suggest detrimental age-related dysregulation of GSH-related metabolites in skeletal muscle repair, particularly γGC, however further examination of the role of exogenous γGC supplementation in this process is required to identify further therapeutic benefit.

title: Extracellular Vesicles Shed from Senescent Neonatal Pulmonary Microvascular Endothelial Cells Contribute to Pulmonary Vascular Remodeling.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are critical mediators of intercellular communication but their role in bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) complicated by pulmonary hypertension (BPD-PH) is unclear. Here we test the hypothesis that hyperoxia induces neonatal pulmonary microvascular endothelial cell (PMEC) senescence and that EVs shed from these cells potentiate pulmonary vascular remodeling. Newborn PMECs exposed to 75% O2 had increased expression of senescence markers and young adult rats exposed to neonatal hyperoxia showed increased p16, p21 and p53 expression in pulmonary endothelial cells. In vivo, EVs isolated from the supernatant of senescent PMECs (senescent EVs) induced pulmonary vascular remodelling and PH in newborn rats. miRNA (miR) sequencing revealed 31 differentially expressed miRs in senescent EVs as compared to control EVs. Top upregulated miRs included miR-421, miR-4508, and miR-3960. Senescent EVs differentially regulated 271 genes in the lungs of newborn rats. The most downregulated gene was myocyte enhancer binding factor-2 (MEF2C), a known miR-421 target, involved in smooth cell plasticity. To further interrogate the mechanisms by which senescent EVs induce vascular remodelling, pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMs) were incubated with control and senescent EVs, and smooth muscle cell phenotype was assessed. Senescent EVs down-regulated MEF2C and induced a synthetic PASM phenotype. EV uptake inhibition and miR-421 antagomir partially restored MEF2C expression and attenuated these changes. Together, these findings demonstrate that hyperoxia induces PMEC senescence and EVs shed from these senescent cells deliver a miR-421-MEF2C signal that potentiates pulmonary vascular remodelling. Strategies targeting this axis may have important implications for the treatment of BPD-PH.
